articles.title: UK engineers built a tiny liquid-metal pump to move robotic butterfly wings and power wearable devices; it could make robots move without bulky motors
articles.summary: Engineers at the University of Bristol have developed a miniature liquid-metal pump weighing just 0.2 grams that could help soft robots move without bulky
articles.body: Engineers at the University of Bristol have developed a miniature liquid-metal pump weighing just 0.2 grams that could help soft robots move without bulky pumping systems. With a volume of 0.086 cubic centimetres, the device can drive a robotic butterfly’s flapping wings, change the colours of a bracelet and power a wearable that squeezes a fingertip to simulate touch. The researchers say the pump operates at less than 1 volt, while the university’s announcement puts its operating voltage below 0.1 volts. The findings, published in Nature Communications on May 12, 2026, could open new possibilities for lightweight wearable devices and flexible robots.How does the liquid-metal pump work?The device, known as a liquid-metal magnetohydrodynamic (LIMA) pump, uses electromagnetic forces to move liquid through a small, flexible channel. Its operation rests on magnetohydrodynamics, the physical principle describing how electrically conducting fluids respond to magnetic fields.The pump contains a tiny droplet of liquid metal, surrounded by sodium hydroxide solution, positioned between electrodes, with a small permanent magnet placed beneath the channel. When current passes through the liquid metal, the magnetic field produces a force known as the Lorentz force. This moves the droplet back and forth, pushing the surrounding fluid and creating a pumping action. In the tests, the current reached about 8 amps at roughly 0.1 volts, for a maximum power draw of 0.8 watts.The resulting flow can inflate or deflate soft actuators, allowing them to bend, contract or move. Reversing the current’s polarity reverses the direction of pumping. Continuous one-way flow requires valves, and the portable version of the system pairs the pump with valves, a microcontroller and an AA battery. There is no impeller or piston, the moving parts of a conventional mechanical pump.A robotic butterfly demonstrates the technologyOne demonstration involved a robotic butterfly whose wings could be raised and lowered using signals generated by the pump.The pump produces a stream of alternating liquid-metal and sodium hydroxide droplets that travels through a tube to a remote receptor. When a liquid-metal droplet bridges the receptor, it completes an electrical connection that activates shape-memory alloy actuators attached to the wings. When a sodium hydroxide droplet passes through, the connection breaks and the wings relax. By adjusting the rate and duty cycle of the droplet stream, the researchers could control the wing-flapping pattern.The pump therefore does more than move fluid, since it also helps transmit control signals to components elsewhere in a soft robotic system. The wings themselves are moved by the shape-memory alloy actuators, not by the liquid metal acting as a motor.A colour-changing bracelet and a wearable touch deviceThe researchers also demonstrated wearable uses. The colour-changing bracelet contains fluidic channels through which two differently coloured liquids can be pumped, and its colour changed in 28 seconds. That shows how fluid movement could alter the look of a flexible accessory without a conventional electronic display.Another prototype combined a wristband with a soft fingertip pouch. Shape-memory alloy actuators in the wristband squeezed the wrist, driven by coded signals from the pump. The finger actuator delivered a gentle pressure sensation through hydraulic pumping and a stronger one through a gas-generating chemical reaction, in which citric acid and sodium bicarbonate pumped together produce carbon dioxide. In its current form, the chemical mode is single-use.In a preliminary test, a blindfolded participant correctly identified the three tactile modes. The timing of each mode was controlled manually with valves, and the authors state that the experiment is a prototype demonstration rather than a validated human-robot interaction study. They say future work will test a larger group of participants.Could it make robots lighter and more flexible?Many soft robots use silicone or elastomer components that move when air or liquid is pumped into them. Conventional systems often depend on external compressors or rigid pumps, which add weight, occupy space and restrict movement. The Bristol design integrates the pumping mechanism into a unit of 0.2 grams and 0.086 cubic centimetres, small enough to distribute through a robot’s body rather than connecting every actuator to a central compressor.The researchers also used the pump to power flexible, jointed actuators inspired by arthropod legs. One of them deflected by more than 45 degrees from its starting position, showing that a very small pump can drive a larger soft component. The pump does not remove the need for other actuators, however: the butterfly prototype still relies on shape-memory alloy to move its wings.Potential applicationsBristol’s press release points to uses ranging from robotic legs to haptic gloves in medical and industrial settings. Firouznia said the pump could be deployed in lab-on-a-chip devices for disease diagnosis, as micropumps for robotic clothing and in tiny actuators for environmental sampling. Study co-author Jonathan Rossiter, professor of robotics at Bristol, said further research is under way on applications from smart bandages to edible robots.What the research foundThe study was led by Saba Firouznia, with colleagues at the University of Bristol and Bristol Robotics Laboratory. It was published in Nature Communications on May 12, 2026, under the title “A flexible liquid metal magnetohydrodynamic pump for soft robotic systems.”The authors report bidirectional flow of up to 70 milligrams per second and a maximum blocked pressure of 3 kilopascals. They say the pump surpasses existing soft and commercial pumps when its output is measured per unit of volume. In a continuous test, it ran for 13.5 hours and 48,600 cycles with only minor drift in actuation, attributed to slight oxidation of the liquid metal. The prototype’s actuation unit costs less than 50 pence in materials.The authors say future work will focus on optimising the design, adding integrated flat valves and simplifying the drive electronics, for instance by replacing the Arduino controller with a simple two-transistor oscillator. For now, the robotic butterfly and the two wearable prototypes offer an early demonstration of how a tiny pump could help flexible machines move, change appearance and deliver physical feedback.

articles.title: University of Glasgow develops £20 ultrasound device to produce fertiliser from air and water, aiming to help farmers in remote areas
articles.summary: Chemists and engineers have developed a £20 prototype device that uses ultrasound, water and air to produce nitrate, an important nutrient for plant
articles.body: Chemists and engineers have developed a £20 prototype device that uses ultrasound, water and air to produce nitrate, an important nutrient for plant growth. The technology could eventually allow farmers in remote areas to make fertiliser on demand, reducing their reliance on large industrial production facilities. According to a study by University of Glasgow researchers, published in Cell Reports Physical Science titled ‘Towards decentralized nitrogen fixation using pulsed ultrasound’, the process builds on a discovery that was first identified in the 1930s and uses sound waves to convert nitrogen from the air into nitrate.However, the prototype remains at an experimental stage. Although laboratory tests have demonstrated nitrate production, the device currently uses proportionately more energy than the Haber-Bosch process. Researchers also need to determine how effectively the nitrate produced by the device can support plant growth.How the £20 ultrasound device produces nitrate from air and waterThe process begins by bubbling air through deionised water for a few minutes to dissolve nitrogen and oxygen. The researchers then use focused ultrasound waves to create tiny bubbles in the water. These bubbles oscillate rapidly and heat up, with the gases in it reaching temperatures of 5,000°C during repeated pressure-driven implosions.The extreme conditions break apart nitrogen molecules and combine them with oxygen to produce nitrate. To identify the most effective method, the team tested different ultrasound settings and used a high-speed camera to observe the bubbles as they oscillated and imploded.The experiments showed that four-millisecond bursts of ultrasound delivered every 80 milliseconds produced the best results, allowing the team to generate nitrate in laboratory tests.How much nitrate can the ultrasound device produce in eight minutesDuring laboratory experiments, the researchers produced a nitrate concentration of around 40 micromolar in 20 millilitres of water over eight minutes. Although the concentration remained relatively low, the results indicate that the process could be optimised and scaled up to produce more agriculturally useful quantities in future tests.Professor Mark Symes of the University of Glasgow’s School of Chemistry said the team wanted to explore whether fertiliser production could be made possible with minimal capital investment for individual farmers. The existing industrial system relies on factories that can cost hundreds of millions of pounds to produce fertiliser in large quantities. The researchers hope their approach could decentralise production and make nitrate available to farmers through a simpler, more affordable process.What makes the £20 ultrasound device different from earlier methodsProfessor Symes asked Dr Lukman Yusuf, the paper’s lead author, to build a working nitrate production system as cheaply as possible using commercially available components. Dr Yusuf developed a working demonstrator roughly the size of a can of coffee beans for about £20.The underlying process was first identified in the 1930s but was never widely adopted for fixing nitrogen from air. According to Professor Symes, advances in affordable ultrasound technology have created new opportunities in sonochemistry, which uses sound waves to drive chemical reactions.The researchers believe their results mark a substantial improvement in sonochemical nitrate production. However, the current prototype remains an experimental system, and further development is required before the technology can be used in practical agricultural settings.How are researchers working to improve the £20 fertiliser deviceThe team acknowledges that its prototype currently consumes proportionately more energy than the Haber-Bosch process. Further research is also required to determine whether the nitrate produced can effectively support plant growth. Dr Paul Prentice of the University of Glasgow’s James Watt School of Engineering said, “Our plan is to spend the next 12 months working intensively to refine the process we’ve pioneered, and reduce the amount of energy it requires.” These developments could help establish whether the technology is suitable for real-world applications. The research received funding from the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council and the Royal Society.

articles.title: Scientists found mysterious lines of holes on the Pacific seafloor; even sediment samples failed to reveal what made them
articles.summary: Scientists exploring the deep sea have discovered unusual patterns of holes in seafloor sediment, but their origin remains unknown despite closer
articles.body: Scientists exploring the deep sea have discovered unusual patterns of holes in seafloor sediment, but their origin remains unknown despite closer examination and sediment sampling. NOAA’s Voyage to the Ridge 2022 expedition observed the formations at depths of about 2,540 metres, with further sightings between 1,440 and 1,500 metres. Researchers documented holes in 2004 along the northern Mid-Atlantic Ridge, north of the Azores. Researchers Michael Vecchione and Odd Aksel Bergstad later examined these earlier observations in a scientific paper, suggesting that the raised sediment could indicate excavation by organisms. Neither investigation established what created the holes, leaving their origin an unresolved question in deep-sea research.What did scientists discover about the mysterious holes on the Pacific seafloorAccording to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, during Dive 04 of the second Voyage to the Ridge 2022 expedition, scientists observed several sets of holes in seafloor sediment at a depth of approximately 2,540 metres (1.6 miles). NOAA described the formations as “several sublinear sets of holes in the sediment on the seafloor”. The holes looked almost human-made, while the small piles of sediment around them suggested that material had been excavated.Researchers attempted to examine the openings using tools attached to a remotely operated vehicle (ROV), but they were unable to look inside or probe the holes successfully. They also could not determine whether the openings were connected beneath the sediment surface. The formations therefore remained unexplained despite direct observations during the expedition.What did scientists find in the Pacific seafloor holesThe formations were observed again during Dive 09 of the same expedition. The holes appeared at four locations during the dive, at depths ranging from approximately 1,440 to 1,500 metres (4,724 to 4,921 feet). The additional sightings allowed the expedition team to collect sediment from holes that appeared to have formed more recently.The ROV pilots used a suction sampler to retrieve sediment, but examination of the recovered material revealed no clues about what had created the openings. A water sample was also collected for later environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis to investigate what organisms might be living in or around the holes. NOAA's report did not identify a confirmed cause for the formations.What did scientists discover about the Mid-Atlantic Ridge holesOn 13 July 2004, a remotely operated vehicle recorded numerous sets of holes during an expedition investigating biodiversity along the northern Mid-Atlantic Ridge, north of the Azores. According to the study published in Frontiers, titled ‘Numerous Sublinear Sets of Holes in Sediment on the Northern Mid-Atlantic Ridge Point to Knowledge Gaps in Understanding Mid-Ocean Ridge Ecosystems’, the observations were made at approximately 2,082 metres below the surface. The researchers described series that were straight or gently curved, with some intersecting or crossing. Individual series ranged from less than one metre to many metres in length. The holes themselves measured approximately 6 centimetres by 1.5 centimetres, based on comparisons with nearby shells. These measurements relate to the 2004 observations, rather than measurements reported for the 2022 expedition.What could have created the mysterious seafloor holesThe sediment surrounding the holes that appeared to be more recent was raised, whereas older holes were partly filled with sediment and had less noticeable raised edges. However, close-up observations did not show living organisms inhabiting the holes, and the researchers could not determine whether the openings were connected below the surface.The raised sediment might indicate excavation by an organism living within the sediment, or digging and removal by an animal on the sediment surface, potentially using a feeding appendage. They also considered whether the formations could be related to the activity of a large bottom-dwelling crustacean, but explicitly stated that there was no evidence supporting that speculation.What are the mysterious seafloor holes calledThe researchers used the term “lebensspuren”, which translates as “life traces”, to describe the formations. The term refers to patterns in surface sediment resulting from bioturbation, the disturbance of sediment by living organisms. Such traces can indicate biological activity even when the organisms responsible are not visible during underwater surveys.The formations resemble ichnofossils reported from deep-marine rocks. Ichnofossils are preserved traces of biological activity, including tracks, trails and burrows, rather than the preserved bodies of the organisms themselves. However, the resemblance does not establish that the seafloor holes were created by a particular species or that they have the same origin as any known fossil trace.What theories could explain the mysterious seafloor holesNOAA invited members of the public to suggest possible explanations for the formations after scientists were unable to determine their origin. Responses included suggestions involving an unknown crab species and gas rising from beneath the seafloor, among other hypotheses. These were suggestions rather than confirmed scientific findings. The sediment sampling conducted during the later expedition did not reveal what made the holes, while the earlier study could not identify the responsible organism or establish how the formations were constructed. Further investigation would be needed to determine their origin and clarify what they reveal about life and sediment processes along mid-ocean ridges.

articles.title: A 2,300-year-old shipwreck off Croatia's Vis island has yielded rare pottery, personal belongings and surviving wooden remains, offering a glimpse into merchant sailing during the Hellenistic period
articles.summary: A shipwreck found off the Croatian island of Vis has revealed an extraordinary collection of ancient pottery, personal belongings and surviving wooden
articles.body: A shipwreck found off the Croatian island of Vis has revealed an extraordinary collection of ancient pottery, personal belongings and surviving wooden remains inside a merchant vessel that once sailed the Adriatic Sea. The 2,300-year-old wreck has brought to light objects that offer a glimpse into the lives of sailors during the Hellenistic period. The findings were announced by the Croatian Conservation Institute on October 4, highlighting discoveries made during archaeological investigations between 2023 and 2025.The shipwreck dates to approximately the fourth or third century BCE, when Greek settlements and local communities maintained extensive trading connections across the Adriatic. It lies in Gnjilna Bay, near the town of Komiža on Vis, an island along Croatia’s Dalmatian coast. Archaeologists initially knew the site through a small number of fragments belonging to Corinthian type B amphorae, large ceramic containers commonly used to transport wine and olive oil. Subsequent investigation revealed that the seabed was concealing more than a scattered cargo of ancient jars.Unique archaeological findsUnderwater archaeologists uncovered parts of the vessel itself, equipment, coins, animal bones, and a remarkable assortment of ceramic objects. Among the most unique finds are nearly six metres of preserved wooden ship structure, finely crafted drinking vessels, pottery bearing possible personal names and a coin dating to the fourth century BCE.One of the most significant discoveries came when archaeologists exposed portions of the vessel's wooden construction. Archaeologists discovered approximately six metres of surviving hull structure, including part of the keel and attached wooden planking. Researchers also recovered a lead component from a ship’s anchor, identified as belonging to the Haldane II A type. Together with the amphora fragments, this object helped establish the shipwreck’s preliminary date.These timbers provide an opportunity to investigate how shipbuilders constructed merchant vessels more than two millennia ago. While pottery can reveal what a ship carried, surviving wooden components offer evidence of the vessel that transported those goods.Another striking aspect of the find is the ceramic collection. Instead of finding the transport containers associated with merchant ships, archaeologists encountered an assortment of smaller vessels connected to drinking, serving and everyday activities. Among the finds are skyphoi, drinking cups with handles; kantharoi, distinctive vessels associated with wine drinking; and askoi, small containers designed for pouring liquids. The collection also includes bowls, plates, salt dishes, and aryballoi, small vessels commonly associated with oils or perfumes.Among the shipwreck’s discoveries is a coin from ancient Pharos dating to the fourth century BCE. Although a single coin cannot establish the vessel’s precise route, it adds another link to the commercial and cultural environment in which the ship operated.The maritime trade of the past The drinking vessels also connect the discovery to the ancient city of Issa, established on Vis during the fourth century BCE. Issa later became famous for its wine, a product that helped shape the island’s economic identity in antiquity.According to the Croatian Conservation Institute, the assemblage represents the first identified shipwreck with finds of Greek fine pottery, making Gnjilna particularly important for understanding the objects that accompanied maritime trade. It provides valuable evidence of the commercial networks that linked Greek settlements, Italian coastal communities, and the eastern Adriatic during the Hellenistic period.A 2022 scientific study by archaeologists Maja Miše and Patrick Sean Quinn examined 248 amphora fragments from 15 archaeological sites across the Dalmatian region, including Gnjilna. Their research, published in Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences, used the composition of the pottery to investigate where ancient transport containers originated and how they circulated through maritime trade networks. The analysis revealed an especially interesting detail about the Gnjilna cargo. Although the merchant vessel carried two different forms of Corinthian amphorae, identified as type A′ and type B, researchers concluded that they originated from the same production workshop.Gnjilna’s cargo belongs to a period when Issa on Vis and Pharos on neighbouring Hvar were becoming important centres of Greek settlement and commerce. These communities maintained connections with populations along the Dalmatian coast, while merchants carried wine, olive oil, and other commodities between ports.The shipwreck now offers archaeologists evidence of the commercial and human sides of a maritime journey along the Adriatic seabed more than 2,000 years ago.

articles.title: Eating only 15-ml olive oil before having carbs can have a positive impact on blood sugar spike, in an experiment on mice scientists are tracing the effect to a combination of digestive hormones and nerve signals
articles.summary: A planetarium designed by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright has reopened to the public in Florida, more than two decades after its projection system
articles.body: A planetarium designed by American architect Frank Lloyd Wright has reopened to the public in Florida, more than two decades after its projection system stopped working. Located at Florida Southern College in Lakeland, the restored planetarium is now offering public shows, school visits and educational programmes with new projection and sound technology.The planetarium is located inside the college's Polk Science Building and is the only planetarium ever constructed from a design by Wright, according to West Orlando News. It is also part of a collection of 13 Wright-designed structures at Florida Southern College, which the institution describes as the world's largest collection of his architecture at a single site.The reopening follows a restoration project involving work on both the exterior and interior of the building. The latest phase included installing modern equipment to allow the planetarium to operate again. The space had been used only occasionally since 2004, when its original projection system stopped functioning.“Florida Southern has long been entrusted with preserving Frank Lloyd Wright’s extraordinary vision for this campus, and reopening the Planetarium allows us to bring an important piece of that vision back to life,” said Dr. Jeremy P. Martin, president of Florida Southern College. “This restoration honors the history of this remarkable space while creating new opportunities for our students, visitors and the broader community to experience it in a meaningful way,” he added.Public shows four days a weekWith the restoration complete, the college has introduced a regular schedule of public shows. Visitors can attend programmes on Tuesdays, Thursdays, Saturdays and Sundays at 3.30 pm.Six programmes will be offered on a monthly rotation. These include Cosmic Adventure, Destination Mars: The New Frontier, From Earth to the Universe, God, Science, and Our Search for Meaning, Oasis in Spaceand Undiscovered Worlds: The Search Beyond Our Sun.The shows cover different areas of astronomy, including the solar system, exploration of Mars, exoplanets and the wider universe. Exoplanets are planets that orbit stars outside our solar system.Each programme lasts approximately 20 to 32 minutes. However, the complete visit will take around 60 to 90 minutes because it also includes an introduction to the planetarium's history and architectural importance.Tickets cost $20 per person. Families and groups of four or more can purchase tickets at $15 per person. Admission to the planetarium is separate from the college's Frank Lloyd Wright architectural tours.The facility will also be used by Florida Southern students and faculty members. Schools, community organisations and other groups will be able to arrange visits and participate in educational activities.The restorationThe reopening follows several phases of restoration supported by government funding and private contributions. According to the college, work on the exterior was funded by the State of Florida and private donors. The interior restoration received support through the federal Save America's Treasures programme, along with private donations.The most recent phase, also supported by State of Florida funding, involved installing a COSM projection system and a Bowen sound system. These additions have made it possible to resume planetarium shows using modern technology while retaining the restored historic space.“Reopening the Planetarium allows us to bring an important part of Florida Southern’s history back to life while creating new opportunities for our students and the community,” said Tory King, director of Tourism Operations & Visitor Experience at Florida Southern College. “The architectural restoration brought the space back, and the new technology now allows us to return it to active educational and public use,” she added.History dating back to the 1950sThe planetarium was included in Wright's original plans for the Polk Science Building, which was constructed between 1954 and 1958. Its first show was held on April 7, 1960.For several decades, it served as an educational facility for the college's astronomy programme. Professors used planetarium shows to explain important astronomical concepts to students, while schools and members of the public could also visit.Traditionally, the facility offered four public shows each year. However, its use became limited after the projection equipment stopped working in 2004.Wright had been interested in designing a planetarium for several decades before including one in his plans for Florida Southern College. His design for the Science Building included spaces intended for public education, reflecting his belief that colleges should provide learning opportunities for surrounding communities as well as enrolled students.

articles.title: Researchers studying 77 children from Bronze Age cemeteries in Serbia found that burial positions often differed by biological sex, suggesting gender-linked funerary customs were observed during childhood about 4,000 years ago
articles.summary: In Bronze Age communities of present-day Serbia, boys and girls did not have the same burial treatments as adult men and women.
articles.body: In Bronze Age communities of present-day Serbia, boys and girls did not have the same burial treatments as adult men and women. Even children who died at a young age received different burial treatment, with rules that distinguished males from females, with the direction of their heads and position of their bodies following different traditions. A new study published in Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences, which analysed 77 children and young individuals from two Bronze Age cemeteries, has confirmed this practice using proteins preserved in ancient teeth.The research examined Mokrin and Ostojićevo, two cemeteries associated with the Maros culture, which occupied parts of present-day Serbia, Hungary and Romania during the Bronze Age. Mokrin was used between approximately 2100 and 1800 BC, while the Maros cemetery at Ostojićevo dates to around 1900–1550 BC. The study also identified six graves that did not follow the usual pattern, raising questions about how these communities expressed gender distinctions during childhood.Males generally lay on their left sides with their heads pointing towards north and their faces turned east. Whereas females rested on their right sides, with their heads pointing south, also facing east. While these differences were already familiar to archaeologists studying adult burials, determining whether the same customs applied to children had remained difficult.Identifying gender through tooth enamelYoung skeletons often lack the physical characteristics needed to determine biological sex reliably, making it difficult to compare children’s remains with adult burial traditions. The new research addressed this problem by using evidence preserved in ancient teeth rather than relying solely on the appearance of the skeletons.Mina Amzirkov of the University of Belgrade and her colleagues examined data from 128 individuals who had not yet completed physical development, ranging in age from approximately 9-12 months to 18-22 years. The researchers established the biological sex of 77 individuals by analysing the proteins preserved in the tooth enamel for 76 and using results from an earlier ancient DNA study for one other. These methods allowed the team to compare biological sex with burial arrangements without assuming that a child’s position in the grave necessarily indicated whether the individual was male or female. The results showed a clear relationship between biological sex and burial customs at both cemeteries, although the strength of that relationship varied.At Mokrin, the direction of the body closely matched biological sex, while the association with the side on which a person rested was somewhat weaker. At Ostojićevo, the pattern was especially clear among the 17 individuals included in the body-position analysis: none of the boys lay on their right side, and none of the girls rested on their left.Six graves that did not follow customDespite the consistency of these customs, six graves at Mokrin differed from the expected arrangement. Four contained boys buried according to the female pattern, while two belonged to girls whose bodies followed the male tradition. Three of the boys were approximately four to seven years old, and their graves were numbered 25, 103, and 236. Photographs from the original excavations show that their skeletal remains were poorly preserved, so the researchers could not rule out mistakes in the recorded orientation of their bodies.The other three graves contained better-preserved remains and presented questions that were harder to resolve. Grave 220 belonged to a boy approximately 10–11 years old, whose biological sex had been established through earlier DNA research. He lay on his right side with his head toward the south, following the female burial pattern, and his grave contained no accompanying objects.Grave 216 contained a girl aged approximately 8–9, buried on her left side with her head pointing north. Her grave also contained no objects, while Grave 238 belonged to another girl, aged approximately 14–15, whose burial included pottery and animal bones. The older girl’s burial became particularly important when researchers returned to photographs from the original excavation. An earlier publication had recorded her as lying on her right side, but the photographs showed that she actually rested on her left, confirming that her burial followed the male pattern.The researchers found no shared characteristic that could explain these three better-preserved exceptions. The children differed in age, grave location, and accompanying objects, leaving open the possibility that their burials reflected circumstances or decisions that cannot now be established.Gender distinctions since childhoodThe study indicates that Maros communities recognised distinctions between males and females from an early age, at least in the way they treated their dead. Children who had not reached adulthood generally received burial arrangements associated with adult men or women, suggesting that these categories were already important during childhood. Other aspects of Maros burial customs also varied according to biological sex and social standing. Weapons were more commonly associated with adult male graves, while ornaments such as necklaces and decorative pins appeared more often in female burials. Children’s graves generally contained fewer objects than those of adults, making body position and orientation particularly useful for studying their funerary treatment.The findings of the research are consistent with earlier research at Franzhausen I, a Bronze Age cemetery in Austria, where scientists found that 62 of 63 children with comparable evidence followed the burial pattern associated with their biological sex. However, the authors emphasise that burial customs cannot establish how individuals understood their own identities or which roles they held during life.The results show that the distinctions applied to adult men and women in Maros funerary traditions generally extended to children as well. Even those who died long before adulthood received burial treatment that reflected the social categories recognised by their community.

articles.title: In 1997, Australia eradicated rabbits from Cabbage Tree Island as part of a wider Gould’s petrel rescue; by 2000 the colony had grown to more than 800 breeding pairs and was producing over 400 young a year
articles.summary: What do rabbits have to do with saving a rare seabird?
articles.body: What do rabbits have to do with saving a rare seabird? On a small island off the coast of New South Wales, their presence was damaging the very habitat Gould’s petrels needed to survive. Getting rid of them became an important part of a much larger conservation effort. In 1997, conservationists successfully eradicated rabbits from Cabbage Tree Island as they worked to protect the seabird and its breeding grounds. According to the New South Wales National Parks and Wildlife Service, conservationists worked to restore Gould’s petrel habitat and establish a second breeding colony on nearby Boondelbah Island. By 2000, the island was home to more than 800 breeding pairs, producing over 400 young annually. The turnaround showed how removing an invasive species, alongside other conservation measures, could help a threatened seabird recover.How rabbits became a problem for Gould’s petrelCabbage Tree Island, near Port Stephens in New South Wales, is an important breeding site for Gould’s petrel, a seabird native to Australia. But the island’s vegetation faced a problem after European rabbits were introduced in 1906. As the animals fed on plants and seedlings, they made it harder for the forest to regenerate. The loss of young vegetation was more than a problem for the island’s landscape. Cabbage tree palms and other plants formed part of the habitat that supported the petrels during their breeding season. When rabbits ate seedlings before they could mature, the island’s natural vegetation struggled to replace itself.The birds were already under pressure from other threats. Surveys carried out between 1989 and 1992 recorded an average of about 220 breeding pairs on Cabbage Tree Island. Annual production was low, with fewer than 50 young reported in the early 1990s. Pied currawongs preyed on the birds, while the sticky fruits of birdlime trees could trap petrels. With several problems affecting the colony at once, conservationists realised that protecting the bird would require more than one intervention. The programme addressed the threats to the birds while also tackling the damage being done to their habitat.The operation that removed the rabbitsThe rabbit eradication campaign reached its decisive stage in 1997. A research paper published in Biological Conservation in 2000 by David Priddel, Nicholas Carlile and Robert Wheeler documented how the operation unfolded. Rather than relying on a single method, the team used a sequence of measures to bring the rabbit population under control. Myxomatosis spread naturally across the island between May and July 1997, reducing the estimated population from around 250 rabbits to 100.Rabbit haemorrhagic disease was released in August 1997 and reduced the rabbit population by a further 55%. In September, conservationists used aerial baiting to deal with the remaining animals. The bait contained brodifacoum, an anticoagulant poison. The team also tracked rabbits fitted with monitoring devices to assess the effectiveness of the campaign. Within 13 days of the baiting operation, the remaining rabbits had been eliminated. Checks over the following six months found no survivors. The operation did have unintended consequences. Researchers recorded the deaths of two buff-banded rails and one pied currawong. Even so, the removal of rabbits eliminated a major source of damage to the island’s vegetation and gave conservationists a better chance of restoring the breeding habitat.By 2000, the numbers told a different storyThe improvement in the petrel colony was substantial. By 2000, Cabbage Tree Island had more than 800 breeding pairs, and the birds were producing over 400 young each year. This was a marked change from the low breeding numbers recorded in the early 1990s. Removing rabbits helped ease pressure on the vegetation, but it was part of a broader recovery programme. Conservationists were also managing predators and addressing hazards associated with birdlime trees. Together, these efforts helped create more favourable conditions for the birds to breed.Still, a growing colony did not mean the species was completely out of danger. Having a large share of the population concentrated on one small island left it vulnerable to events such as severe storms, fires and the arrival of new predators. That concern led to another important step: establishing a second breeding colony.Why conservationists moved chicks to another islandThe New South Wales National Parks and Wildlife Service worked to establish a new colony on nearby Boondelbah Island. The idea was to give Gould’s petrels another breeding location, reducing the risks associated with depending so heavily on a single island. Artificial nest boxes were installed to provide suitable places for the birds to settle. Chicks were then transferred from Cabbage Tree Island as part of the programme.In 1999, 100 chicks were moved to Boondelbah Island, and 95% successfully fledged. A further 100 chicks were transferred in 2000, and all fledged successfully. These results helped demonstrate that the birds could be encouraged to establish themselves at another site. The project went on to establish a breeding colony on Boondelbah Island. Gould’s petrels have also been recorded breeding on Barunguba Montague Island, where monitoring identified up to 77 marked nest sites in 2021, including 17 nests with chicks.A recovery that still needs protectionIn 2009, the NSW government changed Gould’s petrel’s conservation status from endangered to vulnerable. Although its population had improved, its limited breeding distribution meant that continued conservation work remained important. The rabbit eradication on Cabbage Tree Island offers a useful lesson in wildlife protection. Saving the petrel involved looking beyond the bird itself and addressing the conditions that were making survival difficult. Removing rabbits helped protect the island’s vegetation, while predator management and the establishment of another breeding colony strengthened the wider recovery effort.The colony’s recovery to more than 800 breeding pairs showed what targeted conservation could achieve. It also underlined why the work could not stop there: protecting a recovering species means safeguarding both its habitat and the places where future generations can breed.

articles.title: Astronomers combined 16.7 years of gamma-ray data with 4.9 years of FAST radio observations to confirm a 3.2-millisecond pulsar has two companions, including a Sun-like star on a 73.5-year orbit
articles.summary: Some stars live fast, some burn quietly for billions of years, and a rare few find themselves locked in cosmic arrangements that challenge the usual rules
articles.body: Some stars live fast, some burn quietly for billions of years, and a rare few find themselves locked in cosmic arrangements that challenge the usual rules of stellar evolution. Astronomers have now identified one such system: a rapidly spinning pulsar accompanied by a white dwarf and a Sun-like subgiant star. The discovery makes PSR J0435+3233 one of only a small number of known millisecond pulsars residing in a triple-star system, states an online report by the American Astronomical Society (AAS) NOVA.A pulsar spinning at extraordinary speedAccording to the report, PSR J0435+3233 was discovered earlier this year using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST). It belongs to the millisecond pulsar family, completing a rotation in just 3.2 milliseconds. What immediately set it apart, however, was not simply its speed but how rapidly that spin is slowing.The pulsar is losing rotational speed roughly 100 times faster than typical millisecond pulsars in the Milky Way. Such an unusually rapid slowdown points towards a stronger magnetic field than is normally expected and raises questions about how the object acquired its remarkable characteristics.Initial FAST observations also suggested that the pulsar was orbiting a white dwarf once every eight days. Further observations have now revealed that this compact pairing is only the inner part of a much larger stellar arrangement, the report states.Three stars, two very different orbitsResearchers led by Zonglin Yang of the National Astronomical Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences combined 4.9 years of FAST observations with 16.7 years of gamma-ray data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope. Optical and infrared observations from several facilities helped complete the picture.The data confirmed the white-dwarf companion and detected gamma-ray emission associated with the pulsar. More significantly, they uncovered a second companion: a subgiant star with a mass roughly comparable to that of the Sun.The three objects form a hierarchical triple system. The pulsar and white dwarf make up a compact inner binary, while the subgiant circles the pair from much farther away. Its orbit takes about 73.5 years to complete. The two orbital planes are also tilted significantly relative to one another, either almost at right angles or by roughly 54 degrees. Despite the complicated geometry, the system appears dynamically stable over long timescales.A rare window into stellar evolutionMillisecond pulsars are frequently found with companions. Their extraordinary rotation is generally thought to develop when material from a companion star falls onto the pulsar, transferring angular momentum and effectively spinning it up. Finding one with two stellar companions, however, is considerably rarer.The system is particularly interesting because it exists in isolation rather than inside a dense stellar cluster. That makes it plausible that the three stars formed together, rather than becoming a trio through later gravitational encounters. Its early history was anything but quiet. The most massive star would have exhausted its fuel in less than 10 million years before exploding as a supernova and leaving behind the pulsar. For the remaining system to survive such an event, the explosion's kick and the amount of mass lost had to fall within a narrow range. Even without a kick, researchers estimate only about a 35% chance that the system would remain gravitationally bound.Its future should be calmer. The distant subgiant will eventually become another white dwarf, undergoing a much gentler transformation. For astronomers, the system offers something even more valuable: a rare natural laboratory for studying how stars interact, evolve and survive together across immense stretches of cosmic time.Image Courtesy: AAS Nova/Kerry Hensley; background image from Thilina Alagiyawanna

articles.title: Hegseth’s ‘Project Meridian’ is a conflict of interest in the making
articles.summary: Executives like Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey should be treated as vendors whose products we will buy or not based on their performance, as well as their alignment with a smart, realistic security strategy. They are not strategists, and we should not look to them to perform that critical task.
articles.body:
In a speech that covered a lot of ground, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced recently that he was creating a panel called “Project Meridian,” to look at the future of warfare. It will be led by three individuals: Elon Musk of SpaceX, Palmer Luckey of Anduril, and former Georgia House Speaker Newt Gingrich (R-Ga.).

The appointment of Musk and Luckey to head the panel should sound alarm bells on Capitol Hill. Both men lead companies that have received billions of dollars in Pentagon contracts . And if our future strategy relies heavily on automated warfare, uncrewed vehicles and other AI-driven systems, they stand to make tens or hundreds of billions more in the decades to come.

In a rational approach to security, strategy drives budgets, and budgets purchase weapons that fit that strategy. In addition, military personnel, their civilian counterparts, and the growing ranks of government contractors need to be trained to use those systems effectively.

But this textbook version of national defense strategy rarely plays out so neatly. There are disagreements on strategy within the executive branch, including on when it is worth launching wars like the current conflict with Iran. Congress is also generally divided on key issues of war and peace.

In addition, decisions on weapons purchases too often hinge on where the systems are built, not whether they are aligned with a coherent strategy. Congress often adds more units of a given system to the budget than the Pentagon has requested, or prevents the department from retiring systems it sees as obsolete.

A case in point is the F-35, which has hundreds of defects despite first being proposed nearly 40 years ago, and which spends roughly half its time in the hangar being repaired rather than being deployed on actual missions. Yet the Congressional Joint Strike Fighter Caucus , named after the generic term for the F-35 and made up of members with components of the plane built in their districts, frequently adds more F-35s to the budget than the Pentagon asks for.

Or take the littoral combat ship, which was supposed to be a minesweeper, a vehicle for getting close to shore to insert Special Operations forces, and more. The Navy decided that the ship was ill-suited to a potential conflict with China, because it could not easily defend itself from modern high-speed missiles. But members of Congress from the states where the ships are maintained and repaired blocked the Navy from retiring five of the nine ships it had hoped to terminate.

Meanwhile, the Senate ICBM Coalition , composed of members with Intercontinental Ballistic Missile bases or major ballistic missile work in their states, have passed a law stating that the Air Force cannot reduce the current deployed force of 400 missiles. They did this even though experts such as former Secretary of Defense William Perry have called these missiles “among the most dangerous weapons in the world,” because a president would only have a matter of minutes to decide whether to launch them on warning of an attack, increasing the risk of an accidental nuclear conflict provoked by a false alarm.

To add insult to injury, the new ICBM that is under development by Northrop Grumman, the Sentinel, now has a projected cost more than 80 percent more than original estimates.

Given these realities, one might ask, “how much worse can it get?” The answer is, much worse.

While tech moguls like Musk and Luckey promise to build a new generation of cheaper, more effective weapons, they are also competing for major roles in President Trump’s proposed leak-proof “Golden Dome” missile defense system. Experts ranging from the American Physical Society to the Union of Concerned Scientists to the Bulletin of Atomic Scientists have suggested the dome system would be physically impossible and enormously expensive — a trillion dollars or more over the next three decades, according to an estimate by the conservative American Enterprise Institute.

If executives like Musk and Luckey truly want to create an effective defense for less, they should refuse to work on Golden Dome, which, if fully pursued, could be the greatest boondoggle in the history of Pentagon spending — and that’s saying a lot.

Which brings us back to Project Meridian. Putting major weapons contractors in charge of forging a strategy, that, depending on its main outlines, could greatly enrich their own companies is the height of folly. Neither Musk nor Luckey have any background in geopolitics or defense strategy, unless you count making provocative public statements about “beating China” or pledging to ensure permanent American military dominance through the wonders of technology.

No strategist worthy of the name believes that we can bet our defenses on technology alone. An effective defense force should be grounded on well-trained, well-motivated troops who understand the laws of war and understand that their primary loyalty is to the Constitution, not any single president. Technology is just a tool, not the key to winning conflicts or deterring war.

If we want a genuinely thoughtful assessment of the future of warfare, we should recast Project Meridian with leaders who don’t have a financial stake in its deliberations — one that includes scientists, military personnel who have seen combat, experienced diplomats, academic experts, leaders of industries that don’t do business with the Pentagon, and workers from the arms industry.

Executives like Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey should be treated as vendors whose products we will buy or not based on their performance, as well as their alignment with a smart, realistic security strategy. They are not strategists, and we should not look to them to perform that critical task.

William D. Hartung is principal adviser to the Project on Government Oversight.

articles.title: OpenAI math release wipes out early-career researcher programs
articles.summary: Mathematicians are raising concerns about academic credit, collaborative norms, and whether unpublished work fed OpenAI's models
articles.body:
OpenAI's release of more than 700 AI-generated mathematical manuscripts has wiped out research programs belonging to early-career mathematicians, according to Tristan Buckmaster, a mathematics professor at New York University.

"So we've had whole research programs wiped out on Tuesday by their dump," Buckmaster told CNBC's "Squawk Box," according to Business Insider .

Buckmaster also raised questions about whether unpublished work had contributed to OpenAI's results. He noted that researchers routinely submit proposals to funding panels, and that panelists sometimes enter summaries of that work into large language models. "You have to understand, they have access to all our research proposals," he said, according to Business Insider.

OpenAI posted the manuscripts to GitHub on October 6, describing them as the output of an internal model not yet available to outside users. The company said many of the proofs include computer-checkable versions, along with revision and citation protocols. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

Northwestern University mathematics professor Bryna Kra said in an interview with Business Insider that the sheer volume of the release posed a danger to the collaborative spirit that defines the field. "Mathematics is an extraordinarily collaborative field," Kra said. "There is nobody at this company who could possibly give a talk or answer technical questions about any of these results." She warned that mathematicians could become more secretive if they fear that ideas shared informally might be absorbed by AI before publication.

Ursula Martin, a mathematician at the University of Oxford, described the release as "tossing the community a messy first draft and expecting us to clean it up for them," according to Nature . Alvaro Lozano-Robledo, a number theorist at the University of Connecticut, wrote on X that the volume of papers posted simultaneously was "staggering" and asked why the company had bundled so many results into a single drop, according to Nature .

Not all mathematicians viewed the release negatively. Alex Kontorovich, a distinguished mathematics professor at Rutgers University, told Business Insider that mathematical training could grow more valuable as AI reshapes academia. "Mathematics first and foremost teaches people to think clearly and deeply and for extended periods of time on big problems," Kontorovich said. "And I think in the future there will be even more demand for such skills."

OpenAI's math release came after a period of friction between the company and the mathematics community. The company's publication of 722 papers organized into 372 groups followed its claimed solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, which drew disputes over attribution and an open letter from more than two dozen Fields Medal recipients warning that the industry's approach threatened to undermine mathematics as a field. Questions about data use had also surfaced earlier: Andreas Thom, a mathematician whose work overlaps with one of OpenAI's announced results, accused the company of "dishonesty" over its handling of questions about whether his ChatGPT interactions contributed to its model's outputs.

OpenAI said it plans to fund workshops and conferences focused on AI-generated mathematical results and is working to release the model that produced the papers.

articles.title: Astronomers discover second-generation planet made by dying star
articles.summary: Most known planets are first-generation planets, formed when a star is born.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — Astronomers have discovered evidence of a second-generation planet found around a white dwarf, according to a new study published in Nature Astronomy.

Researchers focused on white dwarf star HS 0209+0832, the core remnant of a low-mass star that burned through its nuclear fuel.

They discovered chemical signatures indicating the existence of a second-generation planet, a world formed from the cast-off remnants of the dead star.

Most known planets, including those in our solar system, are first-generation planets, which form from material left over when a star is born.

The team used data from NASA’s Hubble Telescope , which contained roughly 100 chemical features from its first observation of the star in 1999 that could not be identified. They identified the chemicals as likely to have come from the material ejected by the star as it died, noting that the elements they discovered could only be formed under the conditions of a dying star. The astronomers theorize that the materials coalesced into a giant gas planet.

The planet is estimated to be a gas giant about the same size as Jupiter, though it’s rapidly losing atmosphere. The astronomers still believe it is likely to survive as the white dwarf cools.

Once the white dwarf maintains a consistent temperature, NASA reported that the planet could remain in a stable habitable zone for millions of years

The star at the center of IRAS 23077 is not visible because its light is blocked by its surrounding disk, which is viewed from the side. The diameter of this colossal disk is roughly 3,300 times the distance between Earth and the sun, with enough gas and dust to form super-sized planets in far-flung orbits, the U.S. and German researchers reported in May 2024.
