articles.title: Costa Rica releases 13 white-lipped peccaries after an 18-year absence; the animals disperse seeds from 57 plant types
articles.summary: After 18 years without sightings, 13 white-lipped peccaries (Tayassu pecari) have been released into Piedras Blancas National Park in southern Costa Rica
articles.body: After 18 years without sightings, 13 white-lipped peccaries (Tayassu pecari) have been released into Piedras Blancas National Park in southern Costa Rica as part of a conservation project to restore the species. Its disappearance left a gap in the rainforest’s food chain, disrupting the ecological balance. To address this, Osa Conservation is working with the Osa Conservation Area (SINAC) and surrounding communities to bring the species back to the park.According to Osa Conservation, the project took shape in 2023, when researchers began examining the peccary population and earlier conservation efforts. Surveys involving 335 people from 13 nearby communities later confirmed that the animal had disappeared from the area, helping establish the need for its return.13 white-lipped peccaries return to Costa Rica’s national parkThe release of 13 specimens aims to restore the white-lipped peccary population in Piedras Blancas National Park, where the species has not been sighted for 18 years. Its disappearance left a critical gap in the rainforest’s food chain and contributed to an ecological imbalance. The return is expected to benefit both the ecosystem and surrounding communities.Many young people in the region were not even born when the peccaries were last seen in the park. Their knowledge of the animals comes largely from stories shared by older relatives, some of which are linked to hunting. Their stories also bring back memories of a time when jaguar tracks were seen in the forest.According to an interview with Mongabay, tracking and camera-trap data show the herd appears healthy and cohesive, and further translocations are planned this year toward a target of 25 to 30 animals.What steps led to the return of peccariesThe first efforts began in 2023, when Osa Conservation started working with the Osa Conservation Area (SINAC) to examine the status of the ‘chancho de monte’ on the Osa Peninsula. The work also considered conservation efforts undertaken up to that point and their impact.In 2024, the findings helped shape a project aimed at recovering the peccary population in Piedras Blancas National Park for the benefit of its ecosystems and surrounding communities. The plan focuses on restoring the species while bringing together conservation organisations, government institutions and residents.Guido Saborío, Wildlife Manager at Conservación Osa, said, “We are proud to know that, by protecting the natural wealth of southern Costa Rica, we also offer opportunities for local communities through ecotourism and environmental education.”How did surveys help confirm the peccary’s disappearanceDetermining whether reintroduction was necessary required an understanding of the existing peccary population. However, the project faced a lack of up-to-date studies on the species in the area. Researchers therefore turned to local knowledge to establish whether the animals were still present in the park.A total of 335 people from 13 communities surrounding Piedras Blancas National Park took part in surveys. Their responses helped confirm that the ‘chancho’ had disappeared from the area. Community knowledge played a central role in confirming the need for reintroduction and provided the basis for the recovery effort. The involvement of residents also forms part of the wider approach to conservation and the management of the project.White-lipped peccaries help sustain rainforest wildlife and local communitiesWhite-lipped peccaries play several roles in forest ecosystems. They provide food for large felines, including jaguars and pumas, and disperse the seeds of 57 types of plants. Their behaviour also helps create microhabitats. The animals create bathing areas that other species use for wallowing.Their presence can also create opportunities for surrounding communities through conservation and tourism. Osa Conservation aims to bring together government institutions, local communities and conservation organisations to support both ecosystems and the people who depend on them.

articles.title: Rover Perseverance da Nasa bate recorde de distância em Marte | G1
articles.standfirst: A Nasa informou que o rover alcançou esse marco no domingo.
articles.summary: O rover Perseverance da Nasa atingiu 45,2 km percorridos em Marte, superando o recorde histórico do Opportunity enquanto busca sinais de vida antiga no planeta.
articles.body:
O rover Perseverance, da Nasa, usa instrumentos instalados em seu braço robótico para analisar uma formação rochosa na região de Idubi, em Marte, em setembro de 2026. — Foto: NASA/JPL-Caltech

Embora ninguém jamais tenha pisado em Marte, a humanidade conseguiu realizar explorações extensas da superfície do vizinho planetário da Terra por meio de rovers robóticos. Um deles, o rover Perseverance de seis rodas da Nasa, estabeleceu agora um recorde de maior distância percorrida por qualquer veículo em um mundo além da Terra.

A agência espacial norte-americana anunciou que o Perseverance, do tamanho de um carro, percorreu 45,2 km desde que chegou a Marte há cerca de 5 anos e meio, superando a marca de distância estabelecida anteriormente por outro rover da Nasa, o Opportunity, entre 2004 e 2018. Tanto o Perseverance quanto o Opportunity também superaram as distâncias percorridas por qualquer rover que tenha operado na Lua.

O Perseverance, equipado com um conjunto de instrumentos científicos, tem buscado evidências de vida microbiana antiga em Marte — um planeta que, há muito tempo, era mais úmido e quente do que o lugar frio e desolado que é hoje — e coletado amostras de rochas e solo para um possível retorno futuro à Terra.

Desde o pouso em 18 de fevereiro de 2021, o Perseverance tem percorrido a Cratera Jezero e seus arredores, uma área no hemisfério norte marciano que se acredita ter sido inundada por água e abrigado uma bacia lacustre bilhões de anos atrás.

A Nasa informou que o rover alcançou esse marco no domingo, ao se dirigir para uma área chamada Idubi, passando pela região próxima à borda oeste da cratera, apelidada de Lac de Charmes, onde está mapeando alguns dos terrenos mais antigos já encontrados no sistema solar.

Ele é um dos dois rovers da Nasa que atualmente percorrem a superfície marciana, com o rover Curiosity operando na Cratera Gale, perto do equador marciano. O Curiosity já percorreu 38,15 km desde que pousou em Marte em 2012.

Steven Lee, gerente de projeto dos dois rovers no Laboratório de Propulsão a Jato da Nasa, na Califórnia, disse que o Perseverance não mostra sinais de desaceleração.

“O hardware de engenharia e os instrumentos do Perseverance estão em excelente estado, com todos os sistemas redundantes ainda disponíveis. Uma avaliação recente de todos os sistemas concluiu que eles são capazes de operar até bem depois da década de 2030, provavelmente além disso”, afirmou Lee à Reuters.

O rover chinês Zhurong também coletou dados científicos importantes em Marte, operando nas planícies do norte em 2021 e 2022.

articles.title: Meet Justin Bernstein, the 17-year-old Connecticut student who engineered bacteria to make Arctic ice more reflective and explore a way to slow glacier melting
articles.summary: Justin Bernstein, a 17-year-old student from Greenwich, Connecticut, has developed a research project exploring how genetically engineered bacteria could
articles.body: Justin Bernstein, a 17-year-old student from Greenwich, Connecticut, has developed a research project exploring how genetically engineered bacteria could help slow Arctic ice melting. Named a 2025 Davidson Fellow in the science category, he received a $50,000 scholarship for his work on engineering Cryobacterium to produce reflective silica, potentially helping glaciers absorb less solar energy. His project, titled “Implementation of Bioengineered Cryobacteria to Enhance the Glacial Albedo of Arctic Ice to Reverse Climate Change-Induced Rise in Sea Levels”, uses climate modelling to examine the potential impact on ice loss and rising sea levels. Bernstein is an incoming first-year student at Yale University.How Bernstein’s research uses ice-albedo feedback to slow Arctic glacier meltingArctic ice plays a role in regulating how much solar energy the Earth's surface absorbs. White ice and snow reflect a substantial proportion of incoming sunlight, whereas darker surfaces, including exposed ocean water, absorb more energy. As ice melts and darker surfaces become exposed, the additional absorption of solar energy can contribute to further warming and melting. This process is known as the ice-albedo feedback.Bernstein's project focuses on this feedback mechanism. Rather than addressing climate change solely through measures aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions or removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, his research explores whether increasing the reflectivity of glacier surfaces could help slow ice loss. The Davidson Institute's project description explains that the approach is intended to make glaciers more reflective so they absorb less heat and melt more slowly. The research therefore examines a potential intervention aimed at one of the physical processes that can accelerate the loss of Arctic ice.How Bernstein engineered bacteria to produce reflective silicaBernstein's research uses genetically engineered Cryobacterium, a type of bacterium associated with cold environments, to produce silica, a material used in glass. The project incorporates genes from diatoms, a group of algae that naturally produce silica structures. The intended result is a biological system capable of generating reflective silica using dissolved silicon already present in the surrounding environment.According to the Davidson Institute's account of the research, the bacteria could be applied to glacier surfaces, where the silica they produce would help reflect sunlight. The proposed mechanism is to reduce the amount of solar energy absorbed by the ice and consequently slow melting. The project description also states that the bacteria could reproduce independently and continue producing silica through repeated melting and freezing cycles. These characteristics form the basis of Bernstein's proposed approach to maintaining the reflectivity of glacial surfaces without requiring continuous industrial intervention.How Bernstein’s bacteria-based method differs from silica microbeadsBernstein's bacterial approach with the use of silica microbeads, which have previously been considered as a way to increase surface reflectivity. According to the Davidson Institute, these microbeads can be expensive, short-lived and ecologically invasive. Bernstein's proposed method instead seeks to use an engineered biological system that produces silica from naturally occurring dissolved silicon.The approach is presented as potentially low-cost and self-sustaining because the bacteria could reproduce and continue generating the reflective material after introduction to the glacial environment. However, these are characteristics of the proposed research approach, rather than evidence that the technique has already been deployed successfully across Arctic glaciers. The Davidson Institute's profile describes the project and its modelling results, but does not establish that the intervention has been implemented at a scale sufficient to reverse real-world glacier loss.How Justin Bernstein’s model predicts Arctic ice gainsBernstein's project includes climate modelling to examine how increasing glacial reflectivity could affect ice loss. His simulations suggest a potential change from the current net loss of (9.6 \times 10^9) square metres of ice annually to a gain of (2.80 \times 10^9) square metres per year. The research presents this projected change as a possible outcome of applying the proposed intervention.The implications of preserving glacial mass for sea-level rise. By reducing the amount of ice lost, the proposed method could potentially help limit one contributor to rising sea levels and reduce flooding risks for coastal communities. These figures are modelling results reported in the institute's profile, rather than measurements of an observed change in Arctic ice cover. The profile does not provide sufficient methodological detail to independently assess the simulations or establish that the projected gains would occur under real-world conditions.Why Bernstein pursued a biological approach to ice preservationBernstein's interest in the subject was influenced by his experiences in his coastal community, where he observed flooding on roads and pressure on local infrastructure. He explained in his project description that these experiences motivated him to investigate a solution with both local and global relevance.His research considers how biological systems might complement other climate measures. While emissions reduction and climate policy remain important approaches to addressing global warming, the project explores a way to intervene directly in a feedback mechanism associated with ice loss. Its proposed use of engineered bacteria is intended to preserve the reflective properties of ice while longer-term climate measures take effect. The work consequently examines a potential application of biotechnology to an environmental challenge involving glaciers, sea-level rise and coastal vulnerability.What the research could mean for coastal communitiesRising sea levels can increase the risk of flooding in coastal and low-lying areas, with consequences for infrastructure, freshwater supplies, property and local economies. Bernstein's research proposes that slowing glacial melt could help reduce some of these risks by limiting ice loss.Possible wider benefits associated with preserving glacial mass and limiting additional warming, including effects on agriculture, extreme weather risks and long-term water security. These outcomes remain potential implications of the proposed approach. The available profile does not establish that the engineered bacteria have already reduced sea-level rise, prevented flooding or produced measurable improvements in these areas. The research instead presents a possible method of addressing one component of the processes contributing to climate change.Bernstein's research and recognition as a 2025 Davidson FellowBernstein received a $50,000 scholarship after being selected as a 2025 Davidson Fellow in the science category. The Davidson Institute recognises students aged 18 and under through its fellowship programme, which supports young people undertaking significant work in fields including science, technology, engineering and mathematics.His other achievements include winning the United States competition for the Stockholm Junior Water Prize and earning a gold medal at the international Genius Olympiad, according to his Davidson Institute profile. Beyond research, Bernstein volunteers as an Emergency Medical Technician, serving on community ambulances and organising outreach events to introduce children to ambulances and help prepare the community for medical emergencies. He also teaches younger students about the scientific research process, with an emphasis on encouraging curiosity and critical thinking.Bernstein has described the fellowship as motivation to continue using science to develop solutions to environmental and public health challenges. His project on bioengineered bacteria and glacial reflectivity explores how biotechnology could contribute to climate research.

articles.title: A 14-year-old Indonesian conservationist planted thousands of mangroves and helped local women develop sustainable products, linking coastal restoration with livelihoods for fishing communities
articles.summary: Over the past decade, Indonesia has lost an estimated 12.5 million hectares of forest.
articles.body: Over the past decade, Indonesia has lost an estimated 12.5 million hectares of forest. The decline has put the country under significant environmental pressure and contributed to increased coastal erosion, reduced biodiversity and heightened vulnerability to climate-related disasters. Observing the growing environmental challenges in the country, 14-year-old Harley Fatahillah Yodhaloka Sunoto began exploring ways to contribute solutions at the community level. According to a report by Action for Nature, he is the winner of the 2026 Eco-Hero title for founding a campaign centred on mangrove restoration and environmental education.Mangrove WarriorMangrove Warrior, was launched roughly one year ago with the goal of restoring coastal ecosystems while increasing climate awareness among the youth. Harley recognised that the degrading coastlines of Surabaya left low-income fishing families defenceless against extreme weather and severe tidal flooding.The initiative began with him learning directly from coastal farmers in Wonorejo, a community where livelihoods have long depended on healthy mangrove ecosystems. Together, they developed a mangrove nursery system designed to cultivate seedlings before planting them in vulnerable shoreline areas, while also engaging the school community at SMP Negeri 1 Surabaya to support youth participation and environmental education.Through this collaboration, Mangrove Warrior has cultivated, planted, monitored, and replanted more than 31,000 mangrove seedlings across several coastal areas, including Wonorejo, Gunung Anyar, and Keputih. To maximise shoreline protection and carbon absorption, he scientifically matches specific species, including Rhizophora mucronata, Bruguiera Gymnorhiza, Avicennia marina, Sonneratia caseolaris and Ceriops Zippeliana, to their ideal muddy substrates. Backed by his school network at SMP Negeri 1 Surabaya, he is scaling nursery capacity to achieve a cumulative target of 65,000 mangroves by the end of 2026.Restoring mangroves in coastal terrainMangrove restoration requires significant physical effort and persistence. The planting sites are located approximately 13 kilometres from Harley's home, and reaching them often includes navigating thick coastal mud, sharp mangrove roots and water levels that are chest-high. During planting activities, volunteers frequently encounter difficult terrain while working in dense coastal forest environments. Harley himself has experienced scratches and minor injuries while moving through the mangrove roots and mud.Moreover, Harley champions ecological restoration by linking conservation directly to local livelihoods. Recognising that coastal conservation directly affects the livelihoods of small-scale fishermen and vulnerable coastal communities, he leverages mangroves to filter pollutants, restock marine life and safeguard clean water.He also partners with local mothers to turn ecological protection into financial independence. Guided by Kalpataru Award-winning activist Ibu Lulut Sri Yuliani, they process sustainable, value-added products, including mangrove syrup, mangrove soy sauce, natural shampoo and conditioner made from mangrove extracts, mangrove charcoal briquettes used as alternative fuel, hair and face vitamins derived from mangrove resources, and batik created using natural mangrove dyes. This cyclical economic model proves to communities that protecting standing forests yields far greater long-term value than destroying them.Supported by the environmental group Tunas Hijau Indonesia and international organisations like Wahana Visi Indonesia for post-planting monitoring, he often delves into nature-based engineering. He designed the Eco Geniuz Pillow, made from beach-cleanup plastic waste, featuring barcodes that link users to digital climate education. Driven by a passion for robotics, he even designed an award-winning prototype companion robot for children with autism and plans to develop robotic systems to automate future mangrove monitoring. His advocacy has mobilised over 300 field volunteers, educated more than 500 students, and reached nationwide audiences through national television, national newspapers, radio, and the official podcast of the Indonesian Ministry of Environment and Forestry."When forests disappear, we lose one of nature's greatest defences. Real environmental restoration is never easy; it requires patience, courage, and the willingness to stand in deep water and thick mud while pushing forward. Large global problems can feel overwhelming, but starting in your own backyard shows how local action, multiplied by many people, can create global impact. This is a life mission. As long as I am able to plant, I will keep planting. I want to protect Surabaya, Indonesia, and our planet for future generations and for all living things for the rest of my life," he said to Action for Nature.In the future, he plans to plant one million mangroves across the country, establishing a Mangrove Warrior store dedicated to sustainable mangrove-based products along with developing a Mangrove Conservation School where the youth can learn about ecosystem restoration, climate science and sustainable entrepreneurship. "As long as I am still able to plant, I will continue planting. I hope Indonesia and the world remain safe for future generations. Through mangrove restoration, we can help restore Indonesia’s role as one of the lungs of the Earth."

articles.title: Elon Musk becomes biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm elections to Republican groups; surpasses millions he spent during the 2024 Presidential elections; here's where all Tesla and SpaceX CEO has donated $276 million to
articles.summary: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has become the largest known donor of the 2026 US midterm elections after pouring more than $276 million into Republican political
articles.body: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has become the largest known donor of the 2026 US midterm elections after pouring more than $276 million into Republican political groups since July, according to figures disclosed ahead of a key federal campaign finance filing deadline. As per the report by CNBC, the latest contributions also push the Tesla and SpaceX CEO’s known federal political spending in the 2025-26 election cycle to about $366 million, surpassing the roughly $290 million which he spent during 2024 presidential election.Where Elon Musk’s $276 million wentThe largest share of the newly disclosed donations, $158 million, was directed to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing Republican Senate candidates. The figures were provided by Musk's representatives to The New York Times and confirmed to CNBC by a spokesperson for America PAC, the political group founded by Musk. According to CNBC, the contribution ranks among the largest known political donations by an individual in US history.Musk also contributed more than $76 million to America PAC, which has built voter-turnout operations in several competitive Senate and House races. Other major donations include $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, which supports Republican House candidates, $10 million to the Republican Governors Association, and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association.In Texas, Musk separately donated $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group supporting Republican attorney general and Senate candidate Ken Paxton.* Senate Leadership Fund: $158 million, among the largest known political donations by an individual in U.S. history* America PAC: more than $76 million. Musk founded the group during the 2024 election, and it has built a large voter-turnout operation in competitive Senate and House races* Congressional Leadership Fund: $20 million, to the leading super PAC supporting House Republicans* Lone Star Liberty PAC: $10 million, to a group supporting Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton* Republican Governors Association: $10 million* Republican Attorneys General Association: $2 millionTexas Senate race in focusThe Senate Leadership Fund has spent heavily this cycle to defend the Republican majority, including in Texas. There, Republican Paxton is running against Democrat James Talarico. Talarico leads 48.4% to 45.0% in FiftyPlusOne’s polling average as of October 12.Musk’s footprint in Texas has grown rapidly in recent years. Tesla, X and The Boring Company are now headquartered in the state, and SpaceX is expanding its manufacturing and launch operations there.Reversal of earlier remarksThe spending is a sharp turn from Musk’s public comments last year. “In terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” he said in May 2025.At the time, Musk was stepping back after a highly visible role in President Donald Trump’s administration and a public falling-out with the president. The two have since repaired their relationship and have appeared together at several recent events.Musk also keeps deep ties to the federal government through SpaceX, a major NASA and Pentagon contractor. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month named him co-director of Project Meridian, a Pentagon panel studying the future of warfare.The figures were disclosed days before a Thursday Federal Election Commission filing deadline, when political committees must report their third-quarter finances.You use AI every day. articles.title: Exclusive: Giraffe Bio aims its bespoke biomolecules at the looming copper shortage | TechCrunch
articles.summary: As AI data centers and EVs drive up demand for copper, Giraffe Bio has unearthed a $6.4 million seed round to help miners extract more of the mineral.
articles.body:
Between the AI data center boom and economywide electrification, the world will need a lot more copper. By 2040, copper supplies could fall 25% short of demand.

That’ll be a tall order for the mining industry, which boosts production mostly by opening new mines, which is a costly, luck-driven endeavor. Typically, just 0.3% of prospective mines pan out.

A new wave of critical minerals startups have been working on new ways to squeeze more copper out of existing mines using biotechnology, mostly by focusing on heap leaches, where microbes help separate minerals from waste. Endolith has created “Olympic caliber” microbes, Ceibo is working on its own strains, and Transition Metal Solutions has developed prebiotics to boost microbial activity.

Giraffe Bio is taking an alternative approach. The startup develops mineral-specific chemicals to help mines recover up to 5% more copper. In mining, that amount “is really very material,” Alejandro Buffo Sempé, co-founder and CEO of Giraffe Bio, told TechCrunch. Most would be happy with an additional 1% to 2%.

The startup says it can extract more copper because it’s able to engineer compounds specific to each mine’s mineral content.

To bring the technology out of the lab, Giraffe Bio recently raised a $6.4 million seed round led by Orion Industrial Ventures, with participation from BHP Ventures, Twynam, Air Capital, and Baruch Future Ventures, TechCrunch has exclusively learned.

Rather than douse ores with bacteria thought to facilitate copper extraction, the company grows engineered microbes in a bioreactor to produce the bespoke compounds. Those chemicals are then inserted into a mine’s existing process.

“We can leverage all of the biological machinery without having to deal with keeping alive a microbe, which is very complicated in [mining] environments,” Buffo Sempé said.

The startup is beginning with copper, but it says its platform can be tailored to other minerals, too. “The beauty of this is that we can target copper or we can target gold or silver,” he said.

The startup’s compounds are used in a mine’s flotation process. In flotation, chemicals help minerals either float or sink in a bath of water, allowing the operators to skim the desirable minerals off the top. The tighter the chemicals bind to the minerals of interest, the more that can be recovered. “We are extremely good at only picking up the copper,” Buffo Sempé said.

Mines also use chemicals called depressors, which bind to unwanted compounds like arsenic and sink them out of the mix, leaving more desirable products at the top. Giraffe Bio is using the same biotech platform to develop depressors as well, the CEO said.

In addition to improving mine production, Giraffe Bio can supplant toxic chemicals in the flotation process, too.

“Instead of pouring chemicals that are usually very harmful for the environment and so forth, we’re replacing the function that they are providing to the flotation process with a biomolecule,” Buffo Sempé said. “We’re minimizing the friction towards maximizing the output.”

articles.title: Meet Elizabeth Hanechak, the 18-year-old Massachusetts student whose microbial system could convert plastic waste into drinking water and fertiliser, earning a $100,000 scholarship
articles.summary: Many young people are still working out how to change the world, but Elizabeth Hanechak has already started with the plastic choking our planet.
articles.body: Many young people are still working out how to change the world, but Elizabeth Hanechak has already started with the plastic choking our planet. At eighteen, the student from Russell, Massachusetts, designed a microbial system that uses an engineered enzyme and microscopic algae to break plastic waste down into drinkable water and fertiliser materials. Her work earned one of the nation's most prestigious honours for students eighteen and younger. Curious how one young researcher tackles such a huge problem? Read on. This article walks you through her story, her science, and the hopes she carries for communities facing plastic pollution.Who Elizabeth Hanechak is, and how she became a 2025 Davidson Fellow Laureate with a $100,000 awardElizabeth Hanechak, known as Eli, comes from Russell, Massachusetts, and was named a 2025 Davidson Fellow Laureate in the science category, an honour that carries a $100,000 scholarship. According to the Davidson Institute, she was one of three Massachusetts students recognised in 2025, alongside Ethan Yan of Groton and Philip Meng of Andover; the three share $175,000 as part of a program awarding a record $825,000 to 21 students nationwide in its twenty-fifth anniversary year. Hanechak told the Davidson Institute that she plans to earn a doctorate in environmental biochemistry and start her own environmental research company to carry the work into the real world. Away from the laboratory, she is an Eagle Scout who loves spending time outdoors, especially hiking and camping.The recycled ocean plastic bracelet from her grandmother that gave Hanechak a project and a purposeEvery big idea has a starting point, and hers was a gift. Hanechak told the Davidson Institute that her grandmother gave her a 4Ocean bracelet made from recycled ocean plastic. Curious, she researched the company and the serious harm plastic pollution causes, and by the end of that day she had found not only a project topic but also a new purpose, easing the suffering that plastic pollution brings. That sense of mission has shaped everything since. She explained that in the countries most affected, simply getting rid of plastic is not enough. For affected people to fully recover, she said, the waste must be turned into something useful and healthy for the environment, and that belief drives her ongoing research.How an engineered cutinase enzyme breaks plastic down within 24 hours into two toxic building blocksHanechak's system works in two stages. In the first, she modified an enzyme called cutinase by enlarging its active site, the pocket where materials are broken down, so that long, durable plastic chains can fit inside. According to her project description for the Davidson Institute, this lets the enzyme break the plastic apart within 24 hours, returning it to the two chemicals it was originally made from, ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid, both highly toxic. Those compounds are the raw material for the next stage. Hanechak told the Davidson Institute that the project combines modern genetic tools from microbiology with naturally occurring microorganisms. She added that the microbes are inexpensive to replicate, which makes the process an affordable yet effective way to treat large amounts of plastic waste.Microalgae consume the toxic compounds, leaving fertiliser material and a broth that filters into waterThe second stage hands the toxic compounds to a naturally occurring strain of microalgae. Hanechak told the Davidson Institute that the algae consume the carbon atoms in those compounds as food and convert the remaining molecules into biomass that is nontoxic and can serve as a fertilising material. Because every reaction happens in a liquid broth, she explained, the broth can be filtered to produce a source of drinkable water. She hopes the process will help developing communities that lack the infrastructure to manage large amounts of plastic waste, with fertiliser supporting farms, cleared waterways restoring irrigation, and the absence of plastic preventing accidental burning and improving air quality. Her stated aim is to give those communities access to key resources for growth and development while also cleaning up their living spaces.What the Davidson Fellows honour means to a young scientist, and her service work beyond the laboratoryFor Hanechak, the recognition is about more than money. She told the Davidson Institute that the scholarship stands out because it acknowledges the focus and determination she sees as natural in young people. She said it validates "the hard work and sacrifice required" to bring her project to life, and encourages her to keep committing her energy to it even when she faces failure. Her commitments extend beyond science. For the past three years, she told the Davidson Institute, she has volunteered at her local American Legion post, leading two veteran cemetery improvement projects, and she works as a virtual science fair coach, guiding students new to research as they develop projects and prepare for competitions. Together, those details sketch a young scientist who pairs laboratory ambition with service.

articles.title: A super El Niño is brewing: What it could mean for India's winter and summer of 2027
articles.summary: India is heading into winter with a worrying combination: a monsoon that delivered nearly 13 per cent less rain than normal and an El Niño that could
articles.body: India is heading into winter with a worrying combination: a monsoon that delivered nearly 13 per cent less rain than normal and an El Niño that could become one of the strongest on record by December.With the southwest monsoon now over, attention is shifting to the months ahead. Will India experience a warmer-than-usual winter? Could the rainfall deficit affect water supplies and rabi crops? And could the strengthening El Niño increase the risk of extreme heat during the summer of 2027?The concern is not just about temperatures or rainfall. It extends to agriculture, water availability, electricity demand and public health, as the country prepares for the possible effects of an exceptionally strong El Niño.The larger weather story is unfolding thousands of kilometres away, over the equatorial Pacific Ocean. There, an intensifying El Niño is expected to influence global temperatures and rainfall patterns for months to come.What makes El Niño 'super'?To understand why a patch of unusually warm water in the Pacific can matter to a farmer in India or a power grid operator in Delhi, it helps to start with the ocean–atmosphere system that normally keeps tropical weather patterns in motion.Under normal conditions, trade winds push warm surface water westwards across the tropical Pacific towards Indonesia and Australia, while cooler, nutrient-rich water rises near South America. This temperature contrast drives the Walker circulation, a system of rising and sinking air that influences tropical rainfall.El Niño develops when trade winds weaken and warm water spreads eastwards, shifting atmospheric circulation and rainfall patterns worldwide. It is the warm phase of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a natural climate pattern that also includes cooler La Niña conditions and neutral phases. ENSO typically recurs every two to seven years.“Super El Niño” is an informal term for an exceptionally strong event, not an official category. Soumya Dutta, trustee of the Movement for Advancing Understanding of Sustainability and Mutuality (MAUSAM), said, "This super El Nino is already increasing global temperatures, on top of a high base line global average due to Green House Has GHG driven global heating. And its projected to get even stronger till November 2026. So both this winter and the next summer are very likely to be exceptionally warm (with certain belts in the opposite impact zone)."In its October 8, 2026 outlook, the World Meteorological Organization forecast a Niño-3.4 sea-surface temperature anomaly of approximately +3.7°C during October–December, potentially exceeding the 2015–16 peak of +2.6°C. NOAA projected an 83 per cent or greater chance of strong-to-very-strong conditions persisting through January–March 2027.These are forecasts, not confirmed outcomes. Even an exceptionally strong El Niño does not guarantee a failed Indian monsoon or a specific level of damage.What kind of winter lies ahead for India?With El Niño expected to intensify towards the end of the year, one of the immediate questions is how it could influence India's winter weather.For northern India, winter temperatures and rainfall are also influenced by western disturbances, which bring rain to the plains and snowfall to the Himalayas. Their frequency and intensity will play an important role in determining how the season unfolds.What makes the coming months particularly important is that India is entering winter after a rainfall-deficit monsoon. The effects of that shortfall could continue to be felt through water availability, soil moisture and agricultural activity.The immediate concern, therefore, is not simply whether winter will be warmer or colder than usual, but how the developing El Niño could interact with other weather systems and influence conditions through early 2027.Dutta said El Niño was expected to peak around late November or early December, potentially affecting winter rainfall and snowfall in the cryosphere regions. “A snow drought is also possible, as the falling snow melts into rains and flows away, instead of accumulating layer by layer — as future water storage for summer. All these will impact agriculture, drinking water availability and even industrial activities that depend on these Himalayan rivers,” he said.A deficient monsoon adds to the concernIndia's monsoon has left behind a worrying shortfall. The country received 759.4 mm of rainfall between June 1 and September 30, 2026, against the Long Period Average (LPA) of 868.6 mm, a deficit of 12.6 per cent, or roughly 13 per cent, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD). The department said this was the fourth-lowest southwest monsoon rainfall total since 2001.In weather terms, the LPA is the benchmark against which a season's performance is measured: it represents the average rainfall recorded over a specified period, generally calculated using several decades of observations.Put simply, India's rain gauge fell well short of its historical mark, and the deficit matters because the consequences of a weak monsoon can linger long after the season has withdrawn, affecting water availability, agriculture and the months ahead.El Niño was one of the major climate factors in focus during the season. In its first-stage forecast on April 13, the IMD projected rainfall at 92 per cent of the long-period average; its second-stage forecast revised this to 90 per cent. The eventual national total was lower still.The Ministry of Earth Sciences said these forecasts provided advance guidance for preparedness, while noting that the Indian Ocean Dipole and other atmospheric processes also affect monsoon performance.That distinction matters: El Niño can raise the risk of a weaker Indian monsoon, but it does not dictate the outcome on its own. In a December 2024 reply to Parliament, the Ministry of Earth Sciences noted that, among 16 El Niño years since 1950, seven had coincided with below-normal Indian monsoon rainfall. The inverse relationship is stronger in the later part of the season, particularly September.Water, crops and the rabi seasonThe first consequences may be felt in places where rainfall deficits have already strained water supplies. A weak monsoon can mean less replenishment for reservoirs, rivers, ponds and groundwater, although local conditions vary considerably.What matters now is not just the national rainfall total, but where rain fell, how much water was captured and whether it remains available when farmers and households need it.The implications extend to the rabi season, when wheat, mustard, chickpeas and other winter crops are grown. In rain-fed areas, soil moisture and winter precipitation can be especially important. Where irrigation supplies are limited, farmers may face difficult decisions about sowing, crop choice and water use. Warmer conditions can also increase crop-water requirements.Heavy rain was forecast for areas including Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Kerala and parts of Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh during October 15–18. This rainfall is particularly important for Tamil Nadu and other parts of southeastern India.A hotter 2027? The growing health concernWhile the immediate focus is on winter, another concern is whether the effects of a powerful El Niño could extend into 2027, adding to the risk of extreme heat.One of the most alarming estimates comes from the University of Chicago's Climate Impact Lab, whose researchers projected that the developing El Niño could contribute to approximately 4,51,000 additional heat-related deaths globally over the period covered by their analysis. According to news agency Reuters, their estimate for India was around 15,800 additional deaths over six months, compared with a normal year.A co-author told PTI that the analysis used the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' SEAS5 seasonal forecast and a 1996–2025 baseline. Public-health experts have described the estimate as a warning for preparedness, while cautioning that the mortality projections themselves should be treated carefully.The underlying concern is serious: extreme heat can cause dehydration, heat exhaustion, heatstroke and worsen existing health problems. Outdoor workers, older people, children, pregnant women and people with chronic illnesses can face particular risks.A September 2026 commentary in The Lancet by Ruby Lieber, Dann Mitchell and Andy Haines called for stronger early-warning systems, health-system preparedness and research to identify the specific health impacts of El Niño.Electricity: More demand, less supplyExtreme heat also poses a challenge for India’s power system. Rising temperatures drive up demand for air conditioning and other cooling needs, while weaker winds and reduced rainfall can affect wind and hydropower generation.A July analysis by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) estimated that additional cooling demand could reach 10 terawatt-hours (TWh) over a year. Factoring in higher demand and reduced generation from some renewable sources, the report modelled a potential power generation gap of nearly 18 TWh. In its central scenario, meeting this shortfall through additional coal-fired generation could release an estimated 17 million tonnes of carbon dioxide.The pressure could extend to coal-fired power plants themselves, which require large volumes of water for cooling. Dutta highlighted the resulting supply-side risk, “Unfortunately, over 70% of India's electricity generation is from Coal Power plants, and coal power needs huge amounts of cooling water, about 4000 litres per MWhr. So, just as the power demand shoots up due to higher temperatures, the supply from many coal plants might have to be curtailed due to shortage of cooling water. And simultaneously, drinking water shortages will put extra pressure on these water sources, mostly rivers.”Water scarcity could therefore compound the challenge of meeting peak electricity demand. Dutta, a former member of the advisory board of the UN Climate Technology Centre and Network, noted that India’s per capita water availability was just over 1,400 cubic metres a year, below the 1,700-cubic-metre threshold used to classify a region as water-stressed. If a super El Niño intensifies water stress, competition for limited water resources could put further pressure on power generation as well as drinking water supplies.Additionally, a super El Niño could weigh on India’s economic growth by disrupting monsoon rainfall, hurting agricultural output and squeezing rural incomes. Chirag Jain, Partner and Agricultural & Allied Sector Leader at Grant Thornton Bharat, said the key concern was the impact on rural demand, “which continues to be a key driver of India’s consumption-led growth”. He added that sectors with high rural exposure, including FMCG, automobiles, agri-inputs and consumer durables, “could therefore witness slower growth in rainfall-deficient regions over the coming quarters”.

articles.title: Meet Anika Puri, the 17-year-old Indian-American student who built a $300 AI system to spot elephant poachers with over 90% accuracy and won a $25,000 Davidson scholarship award
articles.summary: When darkness settles over a wildlife reserve, spotting a poacher from hundreds of feet above the ground can be a difficult task, even with thermal
articles.body: When darkness settles over a wildlife reserve, spotting a poacher from hundreds of feet above the ground can be a difficult task, even with thermal imaging technology. For park rangers working to protect endangered animals, a missed movement could have serious consequences. Anika Puri, an Indian-American student from Chappaqua, New York, set out to tackle this challenge with an unlikely combination of artificial intelligence, drone technology and a closer look at how humans and animals move. According to a report by the Society for Science, her project, ElSa, short for Elephant-Savior, developed a low-cost system designed to identify potential poachers in nighttime drone footage. The innovation earned Puri a $25,000 scholarship as a 2022 Davidson Fellow, recognising her work in engineering and its potential application to wildlife conservation. Scroll down to read the details of her journey.Turning curiosity into innovationAccording to the online release by Davidson Institute, Puri’s interest in technology grew from an early fascination with building, experimenting and exploring new ideas. From presenting a Lego Mindstorms robot at Maker Faire to developing an interest in drones and earning a commercial drone pilot licence, she approached engineering as a way to turn curiosity into practical solutions. Her focus eventually shifted towards environmental science and the protection of endangered species. During visits to India, she was struck by the continued presence of ivory jewellery and statues in Mumbai markets, despite international efforts to curb the illegal ivory trade. The experience prompted her to investigate the scale of wildlife poaching and the technology being used to prevent it.She discovered that drones equipped with thermal infrared cameras were already helping rangers monitor protected areas after dark. However, analysing the resulting footage remained a challenge, the release explains.Why traditional detection falls shortDrones monitoring wildlife reserves typically fly at considerable heights to cover large areas while working within limited battery life. At around 400 feet, people and animals can appear as small shapes in thermal images, making them difficult to distinguish accurately, states the online release.Existing detection systems often rely on analysing individual frames and identifying objects by their shape. According to Puri’s research, these approaches could achieve accuracy as low as 20% in challenging conditions. Human operators watching hours of footage also face the risk of fatigue and missed activity. Puri approached the problem from a different angle. Instead of examining only what appeared in an image, she studied how objects moved over time.Reading movement through AIThe ElSa system uses machine learning to analyse spatio-temporal patterns in nighttime thermal infrared videos. These patterns include differences in speed, turning radius and movement behaviour, as well as whether an animal moves as part of a herd, adds the report by Society for Science. By examining these characteristics across successive video frames, the algorithm aims to distinguish humans from animals more reliably than methods based primarily on static images.When tested on the BIRDSAI thermal infrared video dataset, collected from four national parks in Africa, the system achieved 90.9% accuracy in detecting humans. The result represented roughly a fourfold improvement over the existing methods cited in her research.Although identifying a human does not automatically establish that the person is a poacher, the technology could help rangers flag suspicious activity for further investigation.Making conservation technology affordableCost was another central consideration in Puri’s design. High-resolution thermal cameras can cost approximately $4,800, placing advanced surveillance technology beyond the reach of some conservation programmes. Her ElSa prototype, built using commercially available components, cost around $300. This significantly lower price point could make automated detection tools more accessible to parks in Africa and Asia, where budgets and resources are often limited. The project offers a glimpse of how artificial intelligence can be applied beyond conventional commercial uses, addressing challenges that affect biodiversity and environmental sustainability.A young researcher with a larger purposeFor Puri, the Davidson Fellowship marked recognition of a project that connected engineering with a cause she cared deeply about. Her work demonstrates how looking at a familiar problem differently can open up new technological possibilities. Wildlife protection requires a combination of trained rangers, effective enforcement, community participation and reliable monitoring. ElSa is not a substitute for those efforts, but it points towards a future in which affordable AI tools could help conservation teams identify threats faster and direct their limited resources more effectively.Images Courtesy: Society for Science

articles.title: Scientists studying 170-million-year-old fossils from Morocco spotted tiny black circles under a microscope; scraping revealed needle-thin teeth from a new crocodile relative that likely ate shrimp and small fish
articles.summary: Sometimes a major scientific discovery starts with something barely visible.
articles.body: Sometimes a major scientific discovery starts with something barely visible. Researchers studying Moroccan fossils found tiny black circles along a long bone. Under a microscope, these markings revealed an unexpected secret: an array of exceptionally slender teeth belonging to a previously unknown crocodile relative that lived around 170 million years ago. The discovery offers a glimpse into the surprising diversity of prehistoric predators during the Jurassic Period, states a release by the University of Portsmouth.A closer look reveals a new speciesThe species, named Ctenosuchus tenuidens, was identified by researchers from the University of Portsmouth in the UK and Hassan II University of Casablanca in Morocco. It belonged to the thalattosuchians, a group of ancient reptiles related to crocodiles that occupied marine and freshwater environments during the age of the dinosaurs.Unlike modern crocodiles, which typically have robust teeth suited to gripping prey, this animal had a long, narrow snout lined with needle-like teeth so fine that they stood out from those of its known relatives. The fossils were recovered from rocks formed in ancient rivers and lakes in what is now the Atlas Mountains of southeastern Morocco. The discovery began when researchers examined the unusual dark markings on one of the specimens more closely. Carefully scraping the surrounding material exposed elongated structures that turned out to be teeth.Special anatomy is reflected in the name. Cteno refers to a comb, suchus means crocodile, and tenuidens translates to thin teeth, a fitting description of the animal's closely spaced dental arrangement.A different-diet predatorTeeth shape and structure revealed Ctenosuchus tenuidens' lifestyle. Using powerful microscopes, researchers examined the teeth's internal features and identified specialised ridges and a tightly packed arrangement.These characteristics suggest that the animal was adapted to feeding on small, relatively soft aquatic prey rather than pursuing larger fish. Its likely diet included tiny fish, crustaceans such as fairy shrimp, worms and other small water-dwelling creatures. The delicate teeth would probably have been poorly suited to gripping struggling, larger prey, which could have damaged them. Instead, the animal appears to have occupied a specialised feeding niche, setting it apart from other long-snouted crocodile relatives.Evolution repeats its experimentsThe discovery also highlights a recurring pattern in evolution: unrelated groups of animals can develop similar features when adapting to comparable food sources. The teeth and jaws of Ctenosuchus tenuidens resemble those of certain ancient aquatic reptiles called mesosaurs, as well as some long-snouted pterosaurs, including Gnathosaurus and Ctenochasma. These flying reptiles lived during the Jurassic and are believed to have used specialised jaws for filter feeding. Such similarities suggest that different prehistoric animals independently evolved comparable feeding adaptations, demonstrating how a shared ecological challenge can produce similar anatomical solutions.Morocco's prehistoric secretsPublished in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology, the research adds to scientists' understanding of the ecosystems that existed in Gondwana, the ancient southern supercontinent that included much of modern-day Africa. It also challenges the familiar image of crocodile relatives as predators built primarily to capture large prey. During the Jurassic, these animals occupied a broader range of habitats and ecological roles than their modern descendants might suggest The fossils from Morocco reveal how much remains to be learned from rocks that have preserved traces of life for millions of years.Images Courtesy: istock and University of Portsmouth

articles.title: In 1941, North Carolina engineers laid a 3,000-foot runway from perforated steel mats in 11 days; by World War II, similar runways could be ready within 72 hours
articles.summary: Explore how North Carolina engineers innovated runway technology during World War II, drastically reducing runway preparation times from 11 days to 72 hours with the Marston Mat. Discover the evolution of prefabricated aviation surfaces and their impact on military operations.
articles.body: An aeroplane is only as useful as the ground it lands on. Soft soil swallows wheels, and a turf field can become badly rutted after sustained rain and heavy aircraft use. For an army that expects to move its aircraft close to the fighting, the time needed to prepare a landing strip matters nearly as much as the aircraft themselves. Conventional paving provides a solution to the problem but requires time, machinery, and plenty of material, which is not something that a forward unit can always have available. This is why engineers developed a prefabricated steel mat. Air Force Magazine notes that it packed tightly for ocean shipment, that one man could handle a section with a sledge, usually the only tool needed to lay it, and that two men with pry bars could remove a single mat.Marston mat development from December 1939 to the pierced design of winter 1940 to 1941The Wisconsin Aviation Hall of Fame traces the development of the Marston mat to December 1939. Early versions tested in the summer of 1940 were solid ribbed steel, and changes over the following winter produced the production design with punched holes. The Hall of Fame lists the panels as 10 feet long, 15 inches wide and 0.140 inches thick, each weighing 66 pounds. The Hall of Fame describes 87 punched holes, arranged in three rows of 29 along the length of each panel, and a slot-and-tab interlock along the edges that held adjacent panels together. Air Force Magazine, in its April 1989 articleMarston Mat, attributes the design to Gerald G. Greulich of the Carnegie Illinois Steel Company, with many contributions from the Army Corps of Engineers. The article adds that the Air Force specified a material of no more than 7 pounds per square foot, while the mat weighed 5.3 pounds per square foot.The Marston strip of November 1941: a 3,000-by-150-foot runway built in 11 days, including site preparationAccording to the Hall of Fame, the 3,000-foot-long, 150-foot-wide runway was built at Camp Mackall near Marston, North Carolina, during Army maneuvers in November 1941. The runway was built in 11 days, a figure given by both the Hall of Fame and Air Force Magazine. Hap Arnold, then Chief of the Army Air Corps, described the event as “the year’s greatest achievement in aviation warfare,” the Hall of Fame notes. This runway did not last. According to Air Force Magazine, it remained in use for only a few weeks before being disassembled and transported in 18 gondola cars to Langley Field, Virginia.What the 11 days covered: grading and moving 50,000 cubic yards of earthThe 11 days were not spent only on laying steel. Air Force Magazine reports that the period included clearing and grading an area of 350 by 3,800 feet and moving about 50,000 cubic yards of earth. Transportation and installation presented logistical challenges. The Hall of Fame adds that in the Pacific, the Navy’s Seabees could build a 5,000-foot-long, 200-foot-wide runway in two days, laying the matting over a rolled surface of crushed coral. Supply soon increased, and Air Force Magazine reports that by December 1941 two factories had manufactured about four million square feet of mat, and that a year later 29 factories were producing it.ANOAA Ocean Exploration feature by Matthew Hanks of the National Park Service describes a National Park Service and NOAA dive project off Guam, where divers found five sections of pierced steel planking off Agat Beach. The feature states that by the end of the war, Seabee crews could clear, grade, plank and complete a 3,000-foot runway in less than 72 hours, and that the planking also let them stabilise sandy beaches quickly so that supplies could move ashore. The two-day, 72-hour and 11-day figures describe different projects and conditions, so they are not directly comparable and should not be read as a steady progression.Replacement in the late 1950s and the matting research that followedThe Hall of Fame notes that as aluminium became more available for non-aircraft uses, an aluminium version of the planking appeared, and that pierced planking was replaced in the late 1950s as aircraft grew heavier and turned to jet power. It adds that during the Vietnam War a solid, corrugated steel mat, the M8A1, was developed to limit foreign object damage (FOD), and that AM2 aluminium matting later replaced it and is still in use today. The same concern with FOD runs through Recent Advances in Matting Technology for Military Runways, a paper that opens with a historical overview of military mats.

articles.title: In Sweden, builders used pulp-mill boiler ash to stabilize sandy forest roads instead of conventional material; field monitoring found it effective and potentially cost-competitive
articles.summary: In Sweden, a groundbreaking study reveals that pulp-mill boiler ash can effectively stabilize sandy roads, offering a cost-competitive alternative to traditional materials. Field trials demonstrate improved bearing capacity and environmental safety, making this an exciting development for the forestry sector.
articles.body: Forestry depends on roads that can reliably carry heavy timber transport. In Sweden, gravel roads can lose bearing capacity during the spring thaw, when meltwater is trapped in the road and the surface softens. Road owners may need to restrict traffic until the road recovers, so upgrading these roads matters to foresters and to the people who maintain them. Pulp and paper mills face a different problem. Many burn bark and other wood residues to produce energy, and combustion leaves ash that has to be disposed of. One option is landfill disposal, but studies have also examined using the ash in road construction. The trials carried out in Sweden for this research explore the feasibility of adding strength to roads through forest industry residue and at what cost.Sörkrånge road in Timrå: 30% Ortviken fly ash in the base layer, June 2009The best known Swedish example is a gravel road at Sörkrånge in Timrå municipality, upgraded in June 2009, as described in a 2021 Energiforsk report on the road’s first decade. The Swedish Forest Agency, the Swedish Geotechnical Institute and Luleå University of Technology ran the project on a road owned by SCA Skog AB. The report states that the fly ash came from the Ortviken paper mill in Sundsvall, where bark and sludge are burned in a fluidized-bed incinerator. Crews milled the ash into the existing road material to form a base layer of 30% ash and 70% road material, with no other binder. The report adds that the ash consists mainly of calcium and silicate oxides, which give it hardening properties.Two years of monitoring by Maria Arm and colleagues, published in 2014The first monitoring results came from Maria Arm and colleagues, whose study, Pulp mill fly ash for stabilization of low-volume unpaved forest roads: field performance, appeared in the Canadian Journal of Civil Engineering in 2014. The researchers used pulp mill fly ash without additives on a low-volume gravel road and monitored it for two years, measuring the achieved ash content, density, water infiltration capacity and load-bearing capacity. Their abstract reports that the ash-stabilised sections performed better than the conventionally upgraded sections and gained bearing capacity over time.Eleven years of follow-up by Désirée Nordmark and colleagues, published in 2022A road that holds up for two years can still fail later, so the same road was studied again. Long-term evaluation of geotechnical and environmental properties of ash-stabilised road, by Désirée Nordmark, Jenny Vestin, Linnea Hansson and Jurate Kumpiene, appeared in theJournal of Environmental Management. The team monitored the road two, six and eleven years after the 2009 stabilisation and found higher stiffness in the ash section than in the reference sections after eleven years. The Energiforsk report explains that stiffness was measured with a falling weight deflectometer in autumn 2019 and spring 2020. On those dates, test section 2 was 24% and 29% stiffer than reference section 1, while test section 1 performed similarly to it.Soil, pore water and vegetation near the road after 11 yearsIn the above-mentioned study, chemical analyses were conducted on samples of road material, soil, pore water and plants. Leaching of potassium, sodium, chloride, and sulfate from the road samples decreased with time. The Energiforsk report puts the average soil pH at 7.9 half a meter from the ash section, against 5.0 to 5.5 at every other sampling point, which it describes as normal for Swedish forest land. The report also found chromium, lead and copper at levels as high as, or higher than along the reference section than along the ash section. The vegetation on the ash section differed chemically from that on the reference section; however, the Energiforsk report states that no trace element reached a concentration that would cause poisoning symptoms in plants. The authors of the study consider the impact on nearby soil and vegetation low and acceptable.Barium is the one trace element that complicates the picture. The Energiforsk report states that it exceeded the Swedish guideline value of 200 mg/kg for sensitive land use at every sampling point, with 573 mg/kg at 0.5 meters from the ash section against 482 and 497 mg/kg at 1 and 2 meters. The concentration was slightly higher closest to the road, which may indicate spread from the ash, but the high values two meters away suggest elevated background levels.Construction costs: 39% to 67% above gravel in Energiforsk’s 2020 mixing trialsThe above-mentioned study notes that construction costs are higher for ash upgrading than for conventional upgrading. A 2020 Energiforsk report by Linnea Hansson and colleagues quantified this on two other test roads west of Timrå, where 20% to 25% Ortviken fly ash was mixed with crushed rock. It found that a base course cost 39% more than ordinary gravel when mixed with a road grader, 58% more with a mixing bucket and 67% more when mixed in a crusher.What one test road can and cannot showOnly the thicker ash layer on test section 2 stayed clearly stiffer than the reference sections, and costs remain higher. Both Energiforsk reports stress that results depend on the ash, the road material and the soil beneath, so more long-term trials on roads built under different conditions are needed before wider use.

articles.title: Tiny Scottish island of Lismore, home to 190 residents, uncovers fresh evidence of a legendary Christian monastery; experts uncover medieval cemetery and over 1,000 artefacts
articles.summary: The residents of Lismore, a tiny Scottish island with around 190 inhabitants, have helped uncover an extraordinary chapter of its early Christian history
articles.body: The residents of Lismore, a tiny Scottish island with around 190 inhabitants, have helped uncover an extraordinary chapter of its early Christian history by raising funds to investigate its monastic past. Excavations led by a professional archaeologist revealed an early medieval cemetery, ancient buildings and remarkable evidence of sophisticated metalworking and craftsmanship. More than 1,000 pieces of metalworking debris were discovered, including crucibles and moulds associated with jewellery-making. The findings suggest that Lismore was an important religious and artistic centre during the sixth and seventh centuries, offering new insights into early Christianity in northern Britain.The discoveries were made after local residents pooled donations and secured grants to fund archaeological work on the island. Although historical records suggested that Lismore had been home to a monastic settlement dating back to the sixth century, physical evidence of its significance had remained limited.The island’s historical society helped drive the project, which uncovered an early medieval cemetery surrounded by a clay-bonded limestone wall, decorated stonework and the remains of early structures near the parish church.The findings have been documented in a study published in the journal Antiquity. The researchers said the discoveries highlighted the site’s importance as a high-ranking ecclesiastical centre in the Insular northwest and revealed its role in early Christian networks associated with the kingdom of Dal Riata.Archaeologists discover evidence of seventh-century jewellery-makingAmong the most striking finds were more than 1,000 pieces of metalworking debris, including crucibles and moulds used to make brooches. Analysis indicated that craftspeople had worked with gold, copper and silver on the island during the seventh century.Robert Hay, the project’s volunteer coordinator, described the discoveries as extraordinary, particularly given the challenging conditions at the excavation site.“We were [excavating] in this really unfavourable, boggy area,” Hay told The Guardian, reflecting on the discovery of the crucibles and the evidence of precious-metal working.The finds suggest that Lismore was more than an isolated religious settlement. Its metalworking and woodworking activities point to a community with considerable artistic skill and access to specialised craftsmanship, comparable to other prominent monastic sites in the region.Saint Moluag’s legacy comes into focusLismore takes its name from the Lios Mor monastery and has long been associated with Saint Moluag, an Irish missionary who travelled to northern Britain in the sixth century. He is believed to have founded churches in the kingdom of Dal Riata as Christianity spread across the region.Although archaeologists cannot conclusively date every structure and artefact to Moluag’s lifetime, the burial practices are consistent with customs from the sixth and seventh centuries. The researchers believe the evidence points to a thriving monastic community with influence extending beyond the island.“The finds strengthen the notion that the parish church is located on the site where Moluag established a church in the sixth century,” the study’s authors wrote.‘We knew practically nothing’ about Lismore’s pastGordon Noble, an archaeology professor at the University of Aberdeen, said the discoveries had significantly expanded understanding of the island’s historical importance.“This was clearly a really important early Christian establishment,” he said, drawing comparisons with better-known monastic centres such as Iona.Noble added that, despite Lismore’s association with Moluag and the presence of an ancient sculptural fragment, little had previously been known about the site.He described the results emerging from the local community’s efforts as “hugely exciting”.

articles.title: SpaceX and Google both said no. Now his software is riding a SpaceX rocket next to Google’s | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Satlyt wants to be the Android of orbital computing, offering open software that works on many companies' satellites, versus SpaceX's closed, all-in-one iPhone-style approach.
articles.body:
The way Rama Afullo tells it, he saw orbital data centers coming.

The Kenyan American engineer previously worked in Google’s cloud computing business before a brief stint at SpaceX’s Starlink communications network in 2024. His experiences convinced him that there was untapped potential for computers in space.

“When I was at SpaceX, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no. When I was at Google, I tried to pitch this internally. They said no,” he tells TechCrunch.

So he left SpaceX and co-founded Satlyt , a new company with headquarters in Sunnyvale, California, and Nairobi, to build software for satellites that he hopes will let many satellites share the work of large computing jobs in space. The company has raised an $8 million seed round, Afullo exclusively told TechCrunch.

The timing looks good for him. SpaceX has since gone all-in on orbital data centers, and Satlyt’s software is set to launch Thursday on a SpaceX rocket alongside the first prototype for Google’s space data center effort, Project Suncatcher.

Unlike SpaceX, Google, or startups like Starcloud and Cowboy Space Company, Satlyt isn’t planning to build its own spacecraft. Afullo’s team is building the software to operate AI models on satellites, comparing his approach to VMware and Snowflake — companies whose platforms let users run complex software without worrying about the underlying infrastructure.

“The folks like SpaceX who are doing orbital data centers — if they are the iPhone, we’ll build Android as a horizontally integrated, open ecosystem,” he said. In other words, Satlyt wants to offer software that works across many companies’ satellites.

Satlyt has already flown its software on two demonstration missions. The initial focus is finding operational efficiencies for spacecraft, which typically depend on flight controllers on the ground to solve any problems that arise. Sending data back to Earth, known as downlink, is expensive and often slow, so using AI to make decisions on the spacecraft can mean real savings, either when resolving anomalies or by processing sensor readings on the spacecraft instead of on the ground.

Earlier this year, Satlyt deployed Google DeepMind’s Gemma AI model onboard a spacecraft operated by Momentus. The model cut the size of a transmission about onboard software errors by more than 60%, the kind of efficiency that Afullo says can save hundreds of thousands of dollars per satellite each year.

A launch will put Satlyt’s software to work onboard a spacecraft built by TakeMe2Space, an Indian startup that builds computing hardware for satellites. The mission involves three customers: NASA, which is paying the company to test protocols for cloud computing in space; Stellerian, a startup focused on space surveillance (tracking objects in orbit) that wants to test image processing workloads; and TakeMe2Space itself, to show the satellite can host other companies’ software.

Right now, few high-powered GPUs are in orbit. For now, the most likely opportunity lies in the kinds of workloads Satlyt is working on. But the company’s next project is to show that it can create a shared computing system — a cloud — spanning two different satellites, which it expects to attempt next year. If successful, it will allow the company to build a true compute cloud in orbit as a third-party provider to spacecraft builders.

The way to think about it is that we turn your satellite into a revenue-generating managed service,” Afullo said.

Satlyt’s seed round was led by Houston-based Non Sibi Ventures, where partner Bernard Harris, who served as a NASA astronaut for more than 20 years, helped ground the firm’s conviction in a novel, space-based business.

One reason the firm invested was that Satlyt doesn’t depend on a highest-octane vision of space data centers, which faces uncertain economics and a launch bottleneck. “We don’t need data centers in space for Rama to be wildly successful, right?” Non Sibi partner Kent Lucas told TechCrunch. “It can just be driven by the number of satellites going up.”

Afullo’s hope is to be live on 20% of satellites by the end of the decade, when he expects virtually every spacecraft builder to be putting GPUs and similar advanced processors in their satellites.

“If you’re putting up a satellite without putting up a GPU on it, at the very least, you’re doing yourself a disservice, right?” he says.

This story was originally published on October 1. Satlyt is among dozens of other startups vetted by TechCrunch and appearing at Disrupt as part of our broader Battlefield competition happening this week in downtown San Francisco. It all kicks off on Tuesday. Learn more here .
