articles.title: Amelia Earhart mystery enters critical phase as explorers zero in on mysterious object
articles.summary: The 17-person Taraia Object expedition team reached Nikumaroro Island to investigate a satellite anomaly that could be Amelia Earhart's Lockheed Electra.
articles.body: The crew searching for Amelia Earhart's missing plane has arrived on a remote Pacific island — and they're getting ready to investigate new clues that could shed light on her disappearance. Purdue University in Indiana announced Monday that the 17-person Taraia Object expedition team arrived at Nikumaroro Island after a five-day journey across the Pacific Ocean. The aptly named team is investigating a mysterious anomaly spotted in satellite imagery that some researchers believe could be Earhart's lost Lockheed Electra. NOAH'S ARK MYSTERY ENTERS NEW PHASE AS RESEARCHERS PROBE DEEP BENEATH SITE The expedition centers on the Nikumaroro Hypothesis, a theory that Earhart's plane crashed near the remote Pacific island. The team arrived shortly after sunset, so fieldwork was postponed until morning. The vessel moved to the island's eastern side for calmer waters overnight as the crew prepared to go ashore at daybreak. On the first day ashore, the team is focusing on "transporting equipment, clearing vegetation and establishing staging operations at the beach and on the south side of the lagoon," Purdue said in its statement. DIVERS BRAVE DEADLY 'MOUNT EVEREST OF SHIPWRECKS' AS FAMED WRECK BREAKS APART "Upon reaching shore, the team will divide into two teams, with one taking smaller transport boats through the Tatiman Passage, a natural opening on the island’s western side, to access the lagoon and place buoys along the way to guide a return trip to the Marin Mainiku at the conclusion of work," the university added. The second team will cut a trail through the island's jungle, connecting the landing site to the southern side of the lagoon. "Staging areas will be established on both ends of the jungle trail to support the first day’s work, before the focus moves to the Taraia Peninsula on Wednesday" — meaning Oct. 14, the statement also noted. The team is operating 16 hours ahead of Eastern Daylight Time, with Wednesday's activities on the island beginning Tuesday afternoon in the U.S. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Earhart disappeared on July 2, 1937, while attempting to become the first female pilot to circumnavigate the globe by air. Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, vanished during one of the final stretches of their trip after departing Lae, New Guinea, for Howland Island. Earhart, one of the world's most famous people at the time, was only 39 years old. In a statement, expedition leader Rick Pettigrew called the prospect of examining the object gratifying. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "It is incredibly rewarding to be this close to completing our inspection of the Taraia Object and potentially solving, at long last, the outstanding mystery of the disappearance of Amelia Earhart and Fred Noonan more than 89 years ago," he said. Purdue has a longstanding connection to Earhart, who served as a career counselor and adviser to women students at the university in the 1930s. The Purdue Research Foundation also helped finance her Lockheed Electra, which she used during her ill-fated final flight. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The university became involved in the latest search after Pettigrew approached the Purdue Research Foundation in February 2025. Purdue spokesperson Trevor Peters previously told Fox News Digital that, if the Taraia Object is Earhart's airplane, the team hopes to conduct a full-scale archaeological excavation next year with the proper permissions. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The eventual curation of the wreckage has been the subject of discussions with [the Republic of] Kiribati, and although nothing has been finalized, ALI [the Archaeological Legacy Institute] and the Purdue Research Foundation share a dream of returning the plane to Purdue to be displayed, consistent with Amelia's original wishes," he added.

articles.title: Forget rockets — Longshot wants to fire cargo into space from a gun. See it at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Longshot is trying to build a gun big enough to make space data centers a reality.
articles.body:
Rockets are, infamously, a real pain in the butt. Our old friend physics forces rockets to be built with almost no room for error, and even then only a small fraction of their weight makes it to orbit.

There are, at least in theory, other ways to do the job — space elevators, centrifuges, or a big chain hanging from a satellite in space and scooping up cargo from Earth. (Blue Origin spent some time thinking about that one before the idea wound up in a Neal Stephenson novel .)

And then there’s an idea dating all the way back to Jules Verne: Use a big gun to shoot a projectile into space.

Longshot Space Technology , a startup based in Alameda, California, is working on exactly that. The co-founders, CEO Mike Grace and CTO Nato Saichek, see an opportunity to take a technology that has already proven its worth and apply it to the pressing need for space launch. The startup has raised about $20 million from venture investors in service of its mission.

When it comes to frontier technology, Grace says, “you can build something that has a lot of novelty, or you can do something really hard. You don’t get to do both.” He points to SpaceX as an example of a company that has “taken classically de-risked technology and scaled it aggressively.” What SpaceX did with NASA rocket research, he says, Longshot will do with multi-injection guns — designs that give a projectile extra boosts as it moves down the barrel — built for World War II and during 1960s research programs.

The idea is to take all the work done by the first stage of a launch vehicle and collapse that into a reusable accelerator on the ground. Picture a steel pipe mounted horizontally over the ground, with tanks of high-pressure gas attached at ports spread across its length. When a projectile is fired and moves down the barrel, the tanks fire off at precise times to accelerate it — to speeds as high as Mach 4, thus far.

The company is currently firing a 70-foot gun with a six-inch diameter at its test site near Barstow, California, and says it can accelerate projectiles up to near-hypersonic speeds. Soon, it expects to start firing a 140-foot-long gun with a 30-inch diameter at its Alameda test site. After that, the company is preparing to build out a 30-inch diameter gun that is 328-feet long, with plans to extend it to about 3,000 feet — making it the largest gun on the planet. It will be capable of launching 220-pound payloads up to speeds of Mach 8, the team says.

These guns will let Longshot keep proving its technology works while also generating revenue from performing hypersonic testing for the U.S. military, which has awarded the company several contracts. Grace envisions building one of his guns on a U.S. military installation like Fort Bliss, where it could be part of the infrastructure for testing the next generation of U.S. interceptors. (And no, the guns don’t need to point up at an angle. Longshot’s projectile is a lifting body, meaning its shape generates lift, so it will aerodynamically gain altitude once it exits the barrel.)

“If you want to practice shooting down a Chinese or Russian hypersonic missile, wouldn’t it be nice not to pay $30 million for that?” Grace asks. “This is a way for half a million, a quarter of a million bucks, of doing hypersonic clay pigeons, throw them and shoot them down, and do it really fast and really cheap.”

The ultimate goal, however, is putting large payloads into space. The team is confident it can scale up its current design to accelerate payloads to as much as five kilometers per second (more than 11,000 mph). That’s fast enough to get into space if the payload, which effectively serves as the second stage of a rocket, has its own propulsion system. But doing that would require a gun 10 kilometers (about six miles) long and nearly 10 feet in diameter. As you might imagine, one problem the company faces is simply finding suitable worksites.

“The hard part is not building the thing, it’s finding a place where they will let you build the thing,” Saichek jokes.

But if Longshot can realize its vision, the math is very attractive: The system is cheap to construct and to fuel, and is highly reusable. Grace expects that if everything works out, they can send payloads to space for a hard-to-believe $50 per kilogram (about $22 per pound). Considering that the much-hyped orbital data center industry needs prices to fall to around $300 per kilogram to get off the ground, that leaves Longshot plenty of room to offer a competitive price.

It will require some modification to launch spacecraft in this form factor and conditions, but at that price point, satellite operators will be willing to try.

articles.title: Noah’s Ark mystery: 3D-printed model of 157-metre Turkey formation created using radar data after researchers drill over 60 feet underground; geologists say it may be natural
articles.summary: A team investigating a site in eastern Turkey believed by some to be the location of Noah’s Ark has created a 3D-printed model of the boat-shaped
articles.body: A team investigating a site in eastern Turkey believed by some to be the location of Noah’s Ark has created a 3D-printed model of the boat-shaped Durupınar formation using ground-penetrating radar data. Located around 29 kilometres south of Mount Ararat, the 157-metre-long formation is being examined by the Noah’s Ark Scans team, which recently completed the first phase of its field investigation, including drilling more than 60 feet beneath the site. Researchers have collected samples for laboratory analysis to look for possible evidence of human activity or decayed wood, although many geologists maintain that the formation is a natural geological feature.The Noah’s Ark Scans team enlisted architectural mapping company FieldTech to create a scale model showing how the formation currently lies beneath the ground. The model was developed using ground-penetrating radar data collected at the site, along with geophysical analysis.In a social media post, FieldTech explained that the red bubbles shown in the model represent underground voids identified through geophysical analysis. The company clarified that its visualisation was based on scientific outputs, including topographical scans and geophysical results.The model offers a visual representation of the features detected beneath the surface, but it does not, by itself, establish that the formation is a man-made structure or that it contains the remains of a biblical vessel.Researchers complete first phase of investigationThe team recently completed the first phase of its field investigation at the Durupınar formation, which included drilling more than 60 feet underground. Samples collected during the process are expected to undergo laboratory analysis to determine whether they contain evidence of human activity or organic material that could point to the presence of decayed wood.Andrew Jones, vice-president of the Noah’s Ark Research Project, told Fox News that the next stage would involve testing the samples.“That’s what we’ll be testing this winter. Just to see if we can find any type of man-made activity or something that suggests decayed wood,” Jones said.The findings from the laboratory tests could help researchers assess the nature of the material beneath the formation. However, any claims about the site's origins would require evidence that can be independently examined and verified.Why the Durupınar formation is linked to Noah’s ArkThe Durupınar formation is a boat-shaped geological feature in eastern Turkey, approximately 29 kilometres south of Mount Ararat. Some Ark enthusiasts believe its shape and dimensions correspond to descriptions of Noah’s Ark in the Book of Genesis.The Noah’s Ark Scans team describes the formation as a 157-metre-long ship structure that it believes matches the biblical account in Genesis 6. The claim remains disputed, and the formation’s resemblance to a boat is not proof that it was built by humans.The biblical story of Noah’s Ark describes a vessel constructed by Noah to survive a great flood. For centuries, explorers and religious researchers have searched for physical evidence of the Ark, with Mount Ararat and the surrounding region attracting particular attention.Claims about evolution draw attentionThe investigation has also attracted attention because of comments made by Lauren Witzke, the team’s director of marketing and fundraising. In September, Witzke suggested that the findings could challenge established scientific explanations of evolution.Posting from the Durupınar site on September 22, she wrote, “Core drilling has begun and the Big Bang Evolutionists are already on damage control mode.”She further claimed that the findings could lead to university curricula being rewritten and Darwinism being dismantled, describing the site as the place “where creation began anew”.These statements reflect Witzke’s views and expectations about the investigation. No findings described so far establish that evolution is disproved or that the formation represents the remains of Noah’s Ark.Geologists question the Ark theoryDespite renewed interest in the site, many geologists consider the Durupınar formation a natural geological feature rather than a man-made vessel. A boat-like outline alone cannot establish the presence of a ship, and underground anomalies detected through radar require further investigation before their origins can be determined.The samples collected during drilling and the results of subsequent laboratory tests may provide additional information about the formation’s composition. Until those results are available and independently assessed, the claim that the site contains Noah’s Ark remains unproven.For now, the 3D-printed model offers a visualisation of the terrain and underground features identified by the research team. Whether the formation contains evidence of a man-made structure will depend on the findings of further scientific analysis.

articles.title: Exclusive: Cambridge Heavy Industries has been quietly building a desktop fusion device | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Fusion power startup Cambridge Heavy Industries is building a small, laser-powered fusion device to fuel the coming wave of fusion power plants.
articles.body:
Fusion power usually conjures images of massive industrial facilities laced with large lasers or magnets, but a startup in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has been quietly building a device that can fit on a tabletop.

The optics of the device were on display behind Yun Kai, co-founder and CEO of Cambridge Heavy Industries , while he chatted with me on a video call. The company has been operating in stealth out of a small lab near MIT, and Kai gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at the technology it has been developing.

“We purposely built a small modular reactor. It’s tiny, it’s benchtop,” he told me. “Because it’s small, it makes everything easier.”

The small size has allowed Cambridge Heavy to experiment and iterate quickly. “The small module nature can enable 50 to 80 experiments, 50 to 80 shots per day,” he said. Data from those experiments will feed simulations that use AI to optimize the design.

That nimble approach has attracted investor attention. The startup recently raised a $6.2 million seed round led by Azolla Ventures with participation from Overlay, Neta Foundation, P3A, MassCEC, and the Rothrock family.

Cambridge Heavy’s fusion reactor uses lasers to compress a fuel target, similar to the groundbreaking experiment that proved controlled fusion reactions could produce more power than they consume. But unlike other inertial confinement designs, Cambridge Heavy’s minimizes the number of lasers required to spark fusion.

The system uses two main lasers to drive ignition. One laser is split into multiple beam lines that deliver light in concentric rings. Those rings of laser light are timed to hit the flat, round fuel target successively, starting from the outside and working in. The first ring starts a compression wave within the target that starts traveling inward. The subsequent laser rings are timed to boost the wave at just the right moment to further compress the fuel.

As the shock wave reaches the center of the target, a laser fires on the target, generating heat and producing a magnetic field. With the right amount of pressure and heat, fusion occurs.

Cambridge Heavy’s design generates high pressures with relatively low laser power, Kai said. The concept emerged from the lab of Keith Nelson, a chemist at MIT. There, researchers used the laser pulses to study materials under extreme conditions. As they ramped up pressures, they realized they were approaching fusion-ready conditions.

In about a decade, Cambridge Heavy plans to develop a power plant from the concept, though that’ll require scaling up the design. It will be larger than the current benchtop prototype, though not quite as large as other fusion power plants. Kai said it should be about the size of two basketball courts, and it will test whether the approach can generate enough energy to support a power plant.

Before that happens, though, Cambridge Heavy plans to use its smaller-scale devices to make tritium, a rare isotope of hydrogen that will be used by nearly all fusion power plants in the works today. Tritium sells for around $30,000 per gram today.

Each power plant won’t need a lot of tritium — on the order of grams per year — but the substance is so rare that only about 40 kilograms exist today. One recent study predicts that without new sources, the fusion power industry will be short by about 28 kilograms in 2054. At current prices, that’s about $840 million worth of tritium.

Fusion startups are in the process of designing fuel systems that will help the reactors be largely self-sufficient when it comes to tritium supplies, though they may need occasional top-ups. But that process could take up to 10 years, Kai said, giving Cambridge Heavy years of potential revenue as it pursues its power plant.

articles.title: Helix Carbon says it can make iron cheaper by recycling blast furnace pollution | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The steel industry is a big polluter, but Helix Carbon can upcycle pollution from blast furnaces to drive down emissions and improve margins.
articles.body:
The iron and steel industries are among the biggest polluters in the world. Plenty of startups have tried to cut the industry’s emissions, mostly by developing new ways to make the metals. Helix Carbon thinks those startups have been going about it all wrong.

“Any attempt to decarbonize the steel industry without dealing with the blast furnace is not going to work,” David Brown, Helix Carbon’s co-founder and CEO, told TechCrunch. A blast furnace is the giant furnace that turns iron ore into the iron used to make steel. Rather than replace blast furnaces, Helix wants to clean them up. Its approach promises to slash the steel industry’s carbon emissions while boosting profit margins for iron producers, a rare win-win for a dirty industrial process.

Blast furnaces have made iron for centuries, using coke, a processed form of coal, to help turn raw iron ore (iron bound up with oxygen) into metallic iron. The burning coke supplies heat for the reaction but doesn’t take part in it directly. Instead, carbon monoxide produced from the combustion does the work of reducing the iron, meaning stripping away its oxygen atoms.

The process releases tremendous amounts of carbon dioxide, or CO 2 , which is normally dumped straight into the atmosphere. But Helix Carbon has devised a way to turn that waste carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide and recycle it back into the blast furnace.

Helix Carbon’s process relies on an electrolyzer, a device that uses electricity and a catalyst to break off an oxygen atom from the carbon dioxide. Electrolyzers aren’t new, but Brown said the startup’s design can handle the entire exhaust stream from the blast furnace. Most electrolyzers are too delicate for raw exhaust like that. They work only on purified, concentrated carbon dioxide, so the exhaust typically has to be processed before they can use it.

By injecting carbon monoxide into a blast furnace, iron producers can use less coke. How much, exactly, is still debated, Brown said. Some scientific papers suggest as much as 90% of the coke can be eliminated, while other studies suggest it’s more like 30% to 40%.

Helix Carbon is proposing that iron producers start by replacing 33% of their coke. The company says using its technology to do so would save them $14 per ton of iron. “That may not seem like a lot, but margins in the iron industry are famously thin,” Brown said.

The iron and steel industries are a combined $2 trillion market, according to Grand View Research , which makes the sector an appealing target for a young startup to chase. But it also moves slowly, in part because its equipment lasts so long. “There are blast furnaces that have lived for over 100 years,” Brown said.

To bring in revenue earlier, Helix Carbon plans to court the specialty chemicals industry first. “We don’t need to capture the CO 2 first,” Brown said. “We just utilize it, and that opens up the door of making chemicals on site right out of waste streams.”

Helix Carbon is part of the Startup Battlefield pitch competition and presented live on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Tuesday. Join us this week to watch as the rest of the Battlefield unfolds.

articles.title: Nevada’s ‘lost’ species raise extinction fears as new journal tracks missing plants and animals; US wildlife agency staffing falls 38% in state, over 4,300 species globally unrecorded for a decade
articles.summary: A rare wildflower once found in the scrublands of Las Vegas has not been reliably recorded in the area for nearly a century, highlighting growing concerns
articles.body: A rare wildflower once found in the scrublands of Las Vegas has not been reliably recorded in the area for nearly a century, highlighting growing concerns about species that may be disappearing before scientists can determine whether they are extinct. The plant, Oreocarya insolita, is believed to exist nowhere else in the world. Now, researchers are documenting such missing plants and animals through a new scientific publication, the Journal of Lost Species, co-edited by University of Nevada, Reno entomologist Matthew Forister. The initiative aims to track species not observed for a decade or more and encourage efforts to find them before they vanish unnoticed.Scientists seek to document species in limboForister and an international team of scientists are focusing on species described as “lost” - those that have not been seen for years but cannot yet be declared extinct. The journal aims to give these plants and animals greater scientific attention and encourage researchers to investigate whether they still survive.“Nevada is a state where so much exploration still needs to be done for biodiversity,” Forister said. “We really don't know the status of Nevada's biodiversity in terms of which species are stable or extinct or lost.”The initiative comes amid wider concerns about biodiversity loss. According to conservation organisation Re, more than 4,300 species worldwide have not been documented for at least a decade.“Everything deserves a memory,” Forister said, explaining why the team wants to create a record of species whose status remains uncertain.The journal is intended to address a gap between established categories such as endangered and extinct. Species that have not been observed for years are often classified as “data deficient”, a designation that can make it harder to generate public attention or motivate searches.“It's really different in terms of motivation and communication in calling something ‘data deficient’ than to call it ‘lost,’” Forister said. “If it's lost it's like, ‘Holy cow, let's go look for it.’ ‘Data deficient’ is important, but it is not that inspiring.”He added that documenting a species matters even if it is eventually confirmed extinct, because it ensures its disappearance is not overlooked.Nevada faces growing biodiversity concernsNevada is home to a wide range of plants and animals, but many face shrinking populations, habitat loss and other environmental pressures. According to the Nevada Division of Natural Heritage, the state ranks 11th nationally for total species diversity and has the third-highest number of species considered at risk, with more than 1,100 plants and animals facing a high risk of disappearing from the state.The state's biodiversity challenges extend beyond species already listed as endangered. Nearly 50 additional plants and animals are federally listed as endangered or recognised as threatened, while hundreds more have six or fewer population groupings in Nevada.Matthew Forister has warned that much remains unknown about the status of the state's wildlife. Scientists may not know whether some species are declining, surviving in small numbers or have disappeared entirely.“Scientists from around the world are warning we're in an extinction crisis,” Noah Greenwald, endangered species co-director at the Center for Biological Diversity, said.The Journal of Lost Species seeks to make these uncertain cases more visible and provide a clearer record for future conservation work.Endangered species protections under pressureThe launch of the journal comes as the US Fish and Wildlife Service faces scrutiny over the number of species receiving federal protection and a significant reduction in staffing. The agency is responsible for determining which plants and animals are added to the federal endangered species list.According to data obtained through a public records request by the Center for Biological Diversity and shared with The Nevada Independent, the agency's Nevada workforce fell from 134 employees in 2024 to 85 in 2026, a decline of about 38%. Nationwide, its staffing dropped from 9,957 to 6,333 over the same period, according to the centre's records.Greenwald said the slowdown in adding species to the endangered list could leave vulnerable plants and animals without the protections they need.Since the Endangered Species Act was enacted in 1973 under President Richard Nixon, the Fish and Wildlife Service has listed an average of 34 species annually. According to the report, the Trump administration had added only three species to the list during the period covered by the investigation, all in the southeastern United States. During Donald Trump's first term, his administration protected 22 species.“Only listing three species in almost two years is just drastically lower than any other administration,” Greenwald said.For comparison, the report noted that the Clinton administration listed well over 500 species over eight years, while the George W. Bush administration listed 62 during its two terms.Jamey McClinton, administrator of the Nevada Division of Natural Heritage, said delays in the listing process can leave species in an uncertain position.“The process of having listings be so significantly slowed down, I think it is leaving room for a lot more ambiguity, and that's something that's not good for industry or for conservation,” McClinton said. “That increases the imperilment for a lot of species that are being petitioned because they're living in limbo.”Nationally, about 400 species are awaiting listing, including more than two dozen in Nevada, according to the report.Habitat changes add to the threatPolicy changes affecting endangered species protections have also raised concerns among conservationists. Earlier this year, the federal administration issued a rule making it easier to destroy habitat occupied by endangered species. Another rule allows economic factors to be considered when designating critical habitat.One example is the Dixie Valley toad, an endangered species whose habitat has been at the centre of disputes over geothermal development and groundwater pumping near the hot springs and wetlands it depends on in Churchill County, Nevada.Earlier in October, 20 states and the District of Columbia sued the Trump administration over changes they said weakened the Endangered Species Act.Conservationists argue that habitat protection and timely federal listings are important for preventing further declines, particularly for species with small or isolated populations.How Nevada’s wildlife disappearedSeveral species that once lived in Nevada have already disappeared from the state, even though some continue to exist elsewhere. Others were endemic to the region and are now extinct.The passenger pigeon, for example, was once recorded in Nevada, with the last known state sighting reported in Humboldt County in 1867. The species later became extinct worldwide in the early 20th century.Other losses were linked to groundwater pumping, habitat destruction and the introduction of non-native species. Several fish species, including the Raycraft, Ash Meadows and Pahrump poolfish, disappeared from their former habitats around the 1940s and 1950s.The construction of dams also altered river systems and contributed to the disappearance of fish species from Nevada. McClinton identified the Owyhee Dam in eastern Oregon as a major factor in ending Chinook salmon migrations into the state. The Hoover Dam similarly contributed to the loss of the Colorado pikeminnow and humpback chub from Nevada.Some disappearances are more recent. The Great Basin ramshorn, a small springsnail, was extirpated from Nevada in the early 2000s, according to McClinton. In early 2024, the Center for Biological Diversity petitioned the Fish and Wildlife Service to protect remaining populations found in a handful of locations in other states. The agency had not listed those populations at the time of the report.Determining that a species is extinct can take years because the classification carries regulatory consequences. Declaring a species extinct can result in its removal from state and federal protection lists.“Both the state and the feds will remove species from their protected lists if they are declared to be extinct,” McClinton said. “This is exactly where [the Journal of Lost Species] comes into play.”Scientists hope the journal will inspire new searchesForister, who co-manages the largest and longest-running butterfly monitoring study in North America, has spent years examining changes in insect populations.Some Nevada butterflies, including the bleached sandhill skipper, are awaiting federal protection, while others, such as the Mount Charleston blue butterfly, are already listed. Research from Forister's laboratory has found that butterfly populations across Nevada are declining by approximately 25% every 20 years.That work prompted him to reconsider how scientists track species that become increasingly difficult to find.“Then I had this revelation,” Forister said. “We weren't doing enough to keep track of these things.”The new journal, developed with conservation organisation Re, will focus on species that have not been documented for at least a decade but have not been confirmed extinct. Researchers hope that giving these species a dedicated scientific record will encourage further fieldwork and help establish whether populations survive.“The number of species where we don't know where they are in the last 10 years is colossal,” Forister said.For scientists, the goal is not simply to record disappearances but also to identify opportunities to find and protect species before it is too late.McClinton said Nevada's distinctive habitats are home to species found nowhere else, making their preservation important to the state's natural identity.“Biological diversity is inherently precious and valuable. These species evolved to survive in these unique habitats with no interference from humans. They're part of what gives these places their unique character,” she said.“Part of what makes it so fun to recreate in Nevada is never knowing if what you're looking at is globally unique.”

articles.title: Not building third runway would be 'missed opportunity', says Heathrow boss
articles.summary: Thomas Woldbye tells the Today progamme it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project, after comments made by the prime minister.
articles.body:
Not building a third runway at Heathrow Airport would be a "huge missed opportunity" for the UK, the boss of the country's busiest airport has warned.

Thomas Woldbye told BBC Radio 4's Today programme it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say whether he backed expansion.

The airport's chief executive said if its owners could not invest in a third runway, the money "will be invested somewhere else in the world", suggesting a decision would be made in the new year.

The Department for Transport said it was reviewing responses to a consultation and was "considering the appropriate next steps".

A spokesperson added that the government supported airport expansion "across the country where this can contribute to growth and opportunity, while meeting the tests on the environment".

They said expanding Heathrow had the "potential to deliver around £40 billion in economic benefits across the country".

Building a third runway at Heathrow has been debated for decades. The project has proved controversial, facing steep opposition from local residents, politicians and climate campaigners.

Last year, then-chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying that "a third runway is badly needed", and that the government could not "duck the decision any longer".

Heathrow Airport is owned by a consortium of investors, the largest of which is French private equity firm Ardian. Others include the Qatar Investment Authority, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and the China Investment Corporation.

"If they cannot invest in Heathrow... then that money will be invested somewhere else in the world," Woldbye said.

"It's not about allocating this money elsewhere. It's private money. It's not public money. So hence, it will not go into the UK. I think that would be really a sad, huge missed opportunity for this country."

A third runway would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway. It is estimated it would cost £33bn to build.

Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built.

This additional traffic would potentially lead to a huge surge in revenue for the airport's owners, and Heathrow has argued the expansion would provide a "huge economic boost" and create jobs.

The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues.

Whether the new-look government still backs a third runway is not yet clear. Burnham, who as Mayor of Greater Manchester opposed the scheme, said he believed the matter was "for London and Londoners".

"I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he said, speaking to the BBC last month .

Woldbye said he hoped the prime minister would "will come along" with the project, pointing out it was backed by the unions.

He added that a third runway was "not just for Londoners". "Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK."

Downing Street declined to comment on Woldbye's remarks.

Questioned about the noise impact on nearby communities of more planes taking off and landing, Woldbye claimed Heathrow had seen a "stark" reduction in noise over the past 40 years and said the "trend will continue".

"My biggest concern is actually the years of uncertainty. And I think it's time that we give them certainty on what we want with this project so that we can move on and they can move on in their lives," he said.

Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at Heathrow

Woldbye told the Today programme he had not yet met the current Chancellor John Healey, but if he did, he would outline that the airport "contributes dramatically to the economy" but that "we are now full".

"That means we will stop contributing or stop growing that contribution. If we want to avoid that, we need to now take this decision, move forward and continue the work of the previous government to move at speed and deliver this," he said.

The Department for Transport said it was still finalising its Airports National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow. It was last updated in 2018.

Woldbye said Heathrow was working on a planning application which has planned to submit in the next couple of years, but said any decision would be guided by government's the national policy statement.

articles.title: Hunton broadband fears after fibre works stop in village
articles.summary: People in the Kent village of Hunton say they have been left without answers after fibre works stop.
articles.body:
Residents in a rural Kent village have raised concerns they could be left without broadband access after fibre installation works stopped.

Work began in August in Hunton to replace existing copper broadband infrastructure with fibre cables, but residents said it stopped after a few days.

Some residents said they had been told they might need to find another broadband provider, but they did not know what was happening.

Kings Hill-based firm Trooli said it had not been possible to extend its fibre network and affected customers had been contacted. Openreach said the old network would close on 31 January 2027 and customers would need to move to a digital phone service by then.

Resident Rodney Ballard told the Local Democracy Reporting Service that Trooli had given notice to some residents that their connections would be terminated, while Openreach had said copper connections would be withdrawn.

"There's no real plan being told to residents how this is going to happen," he said.

Hunton parish and Maidstone borough councillor Mike Summersgill said residents had welcomed the start of installation work but then "all of a sudden the road closure and barriers were taken away".

After work stopped, he said: "My worry is for the single, elderly constituents who rely purely on the landline to keep in touch with family or to be talked to by doctors."

Leah Istratescu, from Staplehurst, who works at Hunton and Linton Pre-School, said reliable broadband was essential for running the school and communicating with parents, adding: "It's really important that we keep them updated."

A Trooli spokesperson said the broadband service had been delivered using Openreach copper infrastructure that was being withdrawn.

The company said it had explored extending its fibre network, but said: "Unfortunately, there are few locations where, because of excessive costs, we have had to conclude this is simply not possible."

Trooli said it had contacted affected customers and advised them of other broadband options.

After some customers said they had been told the copper broadband switch-off would be on 23 October, an Openreach spokesperson said: "Openreach has no plans to switch off services supporting broadband or phone lines in the village this October."

They said: "Decisions about Trooli's services or its fibre rollout in Hunton are for the company and are separate from the closure of the analogue phone network.

"Anyone concerned about their service should speak to their communications provider - the company they pay their bill to - about the options available."

The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology said rural communities should not be left behind in the rollout of faster broadband.

It said: "We are investing billions of pounds to bring internet upgrades to hard-to-reach homes and businesses that would otherwise miss out - including in Kent.

"Where commercial rollout plans change, the government will work with suppliers to explore alternative ways to connect affected communities."

articles.title: Nithya Tammana, an 11-year-old girl from New Jersey built a youth water-conservation network of more than 450 members; her open-source moss filter is designed to remove up to 95% of lead from school drinking water
articles.summary: At nine, Nithya Tammana noticed something happening in her own home that many people might have overlooked: clean drinking water was going down the drain
articles.body: At nine, Nithya Tammana noticed something happening in her own home that many people might have overlooked: clean drinking water was going down the drain while the shower water was being heated. Two years later, the girl from Monroe Township, New Jersey, has built a youth-led water conservation network, developed a nature-inspired filter designed to remove lead from school drinking water, and taken her campaign for water sustainability to policymakers.Her initiative, Save Drop, began in February 2024 with a simple idea - that small, everyday habits and larger infrastructure changes both matter when it comes to protecting water. Today, according to environmental organisation Action For Nature, Nithya leads a growing coalition of more than 450 young people known as “Water Warriors”, conducts weekly environmental leadership sessions and has helped students launch more than 100 local conservation clubs.Her work brings together three strands: preventing water wastage, encouraging communities to change everyday practices, and using innovation to address water quality.“When I realized how much infrastructure, public investment, and energy goes into treating the water that reaches our homes, I knew we had a responsibility to protect it,” Nithya says, in her profile published by Action For Nature.“I want young people to know that environmental protection is connected to fairness, and that clean water belongs to everyone. When we stay consistent and speak clearly, our age doesn't limit our impact- any one of us can change the system.”From a household observation to Save DropNithya’s journey began with a familiar household routine. Before a shower, water often runs until it becomes warm enough to use. During that wait, the cold water can be wasted even though it has already been treated for drinking.For Nithya, this was not simply about a tap being left open. It was about the resources required to make water safe and available in the first place.Save Drop was her response to that observation. One of its central ideas is encouraging the adoption of hot-water recirculation systems, which redirect cold water instead of allowing it to run down the drain while people wait for the shower to warm up.But Nithya did not limit her efforts to asking individual households to be more careful. She also sought policy changes that could make water-saving infrastructure more widely available.According to Action For Nature, she launched a petition calling for such pumps to be mandated in new housing developments. She also wrote advocacy letters to all 50 US governors.The approach reflects a recurring theme in her work: conservation should not depend entirely on an individual remembering to turn off a tap. Changes in infrastructure, public awareness and policy can also influence how water is used.The half-glass idea that asks restaurants to rethink a habitAnother part of Save Drop focuses on a different everyday setting - restaurants.Through her #ServeHalfGlass campaign, Nithya encourages restaurants to serve customers half-filled glasses of water initially and refill them when requested, rather than automatically filling glasses to the brim.The idea is straightforward. When customers are served more water than they need, some of it may remain untouched and be discarded. Offering a smaller quantity first gives customers the option of asking for more, potentially reducing unnecessary waste.Action For Nature reports that the campaign has already persuaded local establishments in New Jersey to adopt the practice. The organisation also estimates that the approach has the potential to save up to two billion gallons of water annually across the United States.That figure is a projected potential, not a measurement of water already saved by the campaign. Nevertheless, the principle behind the initiative is easy to understand: a small adjustment in how a service is delivered can influence resource consumption across many customers.For Nithya, the campaign is another way to make water conservation part of ordinary life, rather than something people think about only during a shortage.BioLayer: a moss-based approach to lead in drinking waterWhile Save Drop works to reduce water wastage, Nithya has also explored the challenge of water quality.Her innovation, called BioLayer, is a nature-inspired, plastic-free filter made using living Sphagnum moss. According to Action For Nature, the filter is designed to remove up to 95% of lead from school drinking water and costs less than $38.Lead contamination is a different problem from water wastage. Saving water helps conserve a resource, while removing contaminants addresses whether that water is safe to drink. BioLayer represents Nithya’s attempt to apply an environmentally inspired design to the second challenge.The use of living moss is central to the concept. Rather than relying on a conventional plastic-based design, the filter uses a natural material as the basis of its approach to lead removal.The stated performance figure is significant, but it needs to be understood precisely: Action For Nature describes BioLayer as being designed to remove up to 95% of lead. Its profile does not provide further details about the testing conditions, the amount of water treated or the independent validation of the filter’s performance. The figure, therefore, should not be taken as a guarantee that the filter will achieve the same result in every setting.Nithya has also made the BioLayer design open-source. This means the design is freely accessible, allowing schools and other interested groups around the world to explore it without having to obtain exclusive permission to access the design.That decision broadens the ambition behind the project. A solution intended to address a public resource problem can have a wider reach when its design is shared rather than kept proprietary.The reported price of under $38 is another part of the idea: making the design accessible is as important to its stated purpose as developing the technology itself.Turning young people into Water WarriorsNithya’s work extends beyond her own campaigns and invention. A major part of Save Drop involves getting other young people to take up environmental action in their communities.Action For Nature says she mentors more than 450 young changemakers, collectively called Water Warriors, and runs weekly environmental leadership sessions for them. She has also helped students establish more than 100 local conservation clubs.Her educational campaigns, multimedia videos and media appearances have reached an estimated one million people globally, according to the organisation.These figures point to a model of youth engagement in which participants are encouraged not merely to learn about environmental problems but to organise around them. A conservation club can provide a local platform for students to discuss water use, share ideas and pursue campaigns in their own communities.For a young person, the challenge of water conservation can otherwise feel distant or too large to influence. Save Drop’s projects offer several possible entry points: a household routine, a restaurant’s serving practice, a school’s drinking-water quality or a conversation with policymakers.The projects also show why Nithya’s work is not limited to a single invention. The moss filter addresses water quality, while the recirculation and half-glass campaigns address wastage. The network of young people helps carry those ideas beyond one individual.Action For Nature describes Nithya as someone who combines engineering curiosity, grassroots mobilisation and policy advocacy in her efforts to protect water as a public resource.Recognition for a young environmental advocateNithya’s work has also brought recognition. Action For Nature named her a 2026 Eco-Hero and listed her as the recipient of the Dr Mary Griffin-Jones Special Award.She has received the New Jersey Governor’s Environmental Stewardship Award and spoken on a TEDx stage. The organisation also identifies her as the youngest-ever delegate in the 70-year history of the United Nations Commission on the Status of Women.More recently, she was named the national winner of the Mott Million Dollar Challenge, a youth entrepreneurship competition. According to Action For Nature, she won at the live finals in Flint, Michigan, after competing against more than 5,300 submissions from across the United States.Her former elementary school principal, Nicole Cirillo, has also commented on the initiative behind her work. As quoted in the Action For Nature profile, Cirillo notes that Nithya did not need a teacher to assign her a project or an adult to suggest a cause. Instead, she noticed a problem, researched it and worked towards a solution.That observation captures an important part of the story. Nithya’s projects began not with a large organisation or a complicated brief, but with questions about how water is used, wasted and protected.She hopes to continue expanding Save Drop globally. Action For Nature reports that she aspires to a future career combining environmental engineering and pediatric ophthalmology.For now, her work offers a clear message about environmental action: protecting water can involve changing a routine at home, rethinking a practice in a restaurant, developing a new design or helping other young people organise around a shared concern. As Nithya puts it, “our age doesn't limit our impact”.

articles.title: NASA’s Perseverance rover has driven farther than any vehicle on another world; after five and a half years on Mars, it has covered 28.10 miles, beating Opportunity’s 15-year record
articles.summary: NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a new record for distance travelled on the surface of another planet.
articles.body: NASA’s Perseverance rover has set a new record for distance travelled on the surface of another planet. On October 11, 2026, after five and a half years on Mars, the six-wheeled rover’s odometer reached 28.10 miles, or 45.22 kilometres, surpassing the 28.06-mile record set by NASA’s Opportunity rover over nearly 15 years of exploration. According to NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Perseverance achieved the milestone on the 2,006th Martian day, or sol, of its mission.The achievement is more than a numerical landmark. It reflects how far robotic exploration has advanced since NASA’s earliest Mars rovers, and it gives scientists faster access to the varied geology of Jezero Crater and its ancient surroundings. Perseverance is now operating beyond the original mission plan, with NASA approving an extended mission that will carry its crater-rim exploration through roughly the end of 2028, as per the report.A record set in half the timeOpportunity held the previous off-world driving record for years. The rover landed on Mars in 2004 and continued operating until 2018, covering 28.06 miles across 5,111 Martian days. Its endurance made it one of NASA’s most successful planetary missions and set a benchmark that seemed difficult to match.Perseverance reached a slightly greater distance in just five and a half years. It covered the distance on its 2,006th sol, meaning it travelled farther than Opportunity did in less than half the time. NASA says the rover has already driven well beyond its original mission requirement of no more than 12.4 miles.The record also places Perseverance ahead of other major off-world vehicles. It has passed the 22.2 miles travelled by Apollo 17 astronauts Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt on the Moon in 1972, as well as the 24.2 miles covered by the Soviet Union’s Lunokhod 2 rover in 1973, as per the report.How Perseverance drives so farA major reason for the new record is Perseverance’s autonomous navigation system, known as AutoNav. As the rover moves, it images the terrain, builds a three-dimensional map of hazards, and plots a route between waypoints selected by engineers on Earth. NASA describes this ability as “thinking while driving.”This autonomy allows Perseverance to move at or near its top speed without waiting for every decision to be made from Earth. In a single Martian day, the rover can cover as much as 1,351 feet, or 412 metres. More than 90 percent of its total distance has been driven using AutoNav, compared with about 5 percent for NASA’s earlier Opportunity and Spirit rovers, as per NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.The difference in computing power is equally striking. NASA’s first Mars rover, Sojourner, assessed the path ahead using 20 measurement points. Perseverance processes 600,000 points with every look, allowing it to identify obstacles and choose safer routes with far greater precision.Exploring ancient terrainThe record-setting drive occurred as Perseverance travelled toward an area called Idubi, through a region west of Jezero Crater nicknamed Lac de Charmes. NASA says the rocks there may include some of the oldest terrain ever explored in the solar system.The terrain is so ancient that comparable rocks on Earth have largely disappeared because of erosion and plate tectonics. Mars does not have tectonic plates, which helps preserve a longer record of its early geological history. At Idubi, scientists hope to find evidence of ancient hydrothermal systems, environments where heated water may once have circulated through rock.Perseverance’s journey has taken it from an ancient lakebed up a fossilised river system and toward the crater rim. Along the way, it found a potential biosignature in a rock called Cheyava Falls, a discovery that makes the rover’s ability to travel efficiently across varied terrain especially important.A legacy of Mars roversPerseverance’s record is the latest chapter in nearly three decades of NASA rover operations on Mars. Sojourner, the agency’s first Mars rover, travelled about 330 feet during its 83-sol mission in 1997. The twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity arrived in 2004 with planned prime missions of 90 sols, but both far exceeded expectations.Spirit logged 4.8 miles before it was silenced by the Martian winter in 2010. Opportunity continued for 5,111 sols, completed the first extraterrestrial marathon in 2015, and set the distance record that Perseverance has now broken.NASA’s Curiosity rover remains active as well. Since landing in Gale Crater in 2012, it has travelled more than 23.65 miles. Together, these missions show a steady improvement in rover durability, mobility, and scientific capability.What the record means for scienceDistance is only part of the achievement. Longer and faster drives allow Perseverance to examine more rock formations, collect samples from more environments, and build a broader picture of Mars’ past. NASA says the rover’s reach has already carried it from an ancient lakebed to a fossilised river system and then to the crater rim.So far, Perseverance has collected 29 rock and regolith samples from the crater floor, a former river delta, and the crater rim. In the rim region, it is studying impact-generated rocks that are about 4 billion years old, preserving a chapter of planetary history that has been almost entirely erased on Earth.After exploring Lac de Charmes, the rover will continue along the crater rim and head south toward Rainbow Falls, a 328-foot-wide block of ancient crust uplifted by the impact that formed Jezero Crater.The record is not finishedNASA expects Perseverance to continue adding to the record. Project manager Steven Lee said the rover’s mobility systems remain fully operational and that extended ground-life testing suggests it can keep driving for many years. The mission’s first extension began in October and will support exploration of the crater rim through approximately the end of 2028.Engineers are also looking for ways to extend the rover’s working day. Bright glare in its navigation cameras currently forces the team to stop driving by mid-afternoon when the rover is heading toward the Sun. Future software improvements could help the rover see past those visual artefacts, potentially allowing later missions to drive for longer periods each day.For now, Perseverance holds the off-world driving record, but its journey is far from over. Each additional mile brings scientists closer to understanding whether Mars once offered conditions suitable for life, and how its ancient landscapes changed over billions of years.

articles.title: Researchers found that polyethylene microplastics worsened signs of fatty liver, especially when combined with an unhealthy diet, raising questions about a plastic used in everyday packaging
articles.summary: Polyethylene, one of the most widely produced plastics in the world, may have implications for liver health, according to new research from Texas A&M
articles.body: Polyethylene, one of the most widely produced plastics in the world, may have implications for liver health, according to new research from Texas A&M University. The study, published in October 2026 and highlighted by the university’s College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, found that exposure to polyethylene microplastics was associated with signs of fatty liver disease, with more pronounced effects when exposure coincided with a diet high in fat, fructose and cholesterol. The findings add to a growing body of research examining how tiny plastic particles interact with biological systems. While microplastics have been detected in the environment and human tissues, their long-term effects on health remain incompletely understood.How polyethylene may affect liver healthPolyethylene is commonly used in food wrappers, storage containers, packaging and the linings of some disposable cups. Its widespread use makes understanding its potential health effects an important area of investigation.Researchers led by Adi Joshi, an associate professor in Texas A&M’s Department of Veterinary Physiology and Pharmacology, examined whether polyethylene microplastics could influence the development of fatty liver disease. The condition occurs when excess fat accumulates in the liver. It can range from relatively mild fat buildup to more serious disease involving inflammation, tissue damage and, in some cases, scarring.According to the researchers, polyethylene exposure increased indicators of fatty liver disease even without an unhealthy diet. When the exposure was combined with a diet rich in fat, fructose and cholesterol, the signs became more severe. The results suggest that environmental exposures and dietary risk factors may interact, although the findings do not establish how much polyethylene exposure contributes to liver disease in people.Scientists investigate the biological mechanismsTo understand how the plastic might affect the liver, the research team collaborated with scientists at the University of Oklahoma and used a technique known as spatial transcriptomics. The method allows researchers to examine gene activity while preserving information about where changes occur within a tissue. This can help identify specific regions of an organ affected by an exposure, rather than treating the entire tissue as biologically uniform.The analysis highlighted changes involving PPAR-alpha, a protein that helps regulate the breakdown and use of fats in the liver. The researchers also identified ANXA2, a gene associated with cellular processes including tissue repair, as a possible contributor to the observed effects These findings offer potential clues about how polyethylene exposure may alter the liver’s metabolic and protective processes. However, identifying these pathways does not by itself establish that they cause disease, and further work will be needed to determine their precise roles.An unhealthy diet may compound the effectsFatty liver disease has multiple risk factors, including obesity, metabolic disorders and dietary patterns associated with excess calorie intake. The Texas A&M findings raise the possibility that exposure to certain environmental pollutants could add to existing risks.The researchers observed more pronounced signs of disease when polyethylene exposure occurred alongside a diet high in fat, fructose and cholesterol. This is particularly relevant to research into metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, or MASLD, the current medical term for the condition formerly widely known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.However, the study should not be interpreted as proof that eating packaged food or encountering polyethylene in daily life will cause fatty liver disease. The effects observed under experimental conditions may not directly reflect the doses, exposure routes or long-term outcomes experienced by humans.What the findings mean for future researchThe research team plans to investigate whether polyethylene exposure could contribute to more advanced liver damage, including fibrosis, in which persistent injury leads to scar tissue formation. Scientists also intend to explore the molecular pathways identified in the study, including whether changes involving PPAR-alpha could offer clues for protecting liver tissue against potential microplastic-related damage.Another key question is whether other types of microplastics produce similar effects. Different plastics can vary in their chemical composition, physical properties and interactions with biological systems, meaning the findings for polyethylene cannot automatically be applied to every plastic material. For now, the study offers experimental evidence of a possible link between a common plastic and changes associated with fatty liver disease. Establishing the implications for human health will require further research into real-world exposure levels, biological mechanisms and long-term outcomes.

articles.title: Scientists compared lightning from 16 major eruptions between 2010 and 2024 and found it usually peaked 0.5 to 2 hours after the first flash, averaging 1.1 hours, while wider ash plumes kept it going longer
articles.summary: Explosive volcanic eruptions often come with intense electrical activity, known as volcanogenic lightning.
articles.body: Explosive volcanic eruptions often come with intense electrical activity, known as volcanogenic lightning. The team analysed 16 eruptions with a Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) of 4 or above between 2010 and 2024. They used detections from the World-Wide Lightning Location Network and precipitation estimates from the Global Precipitation Measurement mission. According to the study published in Earth and Planetary Physics, titled ‘Implications from lightning detection on the dynamic evolution of volcanogenic lightning due to major volcanic eruptions’, the results showed that lightning generally peaked 0.5 to 2.0 hours after the first registration of volcanic lightning, with an average delay of approximately 1.1 hours. The authors also reported that eruptions with larger ash dispersal areas produced longer-lasting electrical activity.What did scientists discover about lightning from 16 major volcanic eruptionsThe researchers focused on explosive eruptions with a VEI of 4 or higher, because such events typically produce sustained eruption plumes, extensive ash clouds and significant electrical activity. Eruptions were selected mainly from the Smithsonian Institution's Global Volcanism Program. 18 eruptions of VEI 4 or above since 2010 were mapped, all located at the boundary zones of three major plates, mostly along the Pacific Rim. Oceanic volcanoes, including those on islands or the seabed, accounted for about 55 per cent of them. The analysis narrowed to 16 eruptions because the World-Wide Lightning Location Network did not detect noticeable lightning for two of them, Eyjafjallajökull in 2010 and Sheveluch in 2023, both at high latitudes. The network locates lightning from very low-frequency or low-frequency radio signals, with a location accuracy typically within 10 km. Its detection efficiency has been relatively steady since a 2010 upgrade but still varies with region, network configuration and lightning features. Duration was measured in 15-minute windows, beginning one hour before each eruption.Why did volcanic lightning peak 1.1 hours after major eruptionsPeak lightning activity lagged the main eruption by a time ranging mainly from 0.5 to 2.0 hours, with a mean lag of approximately 1.1 hours. The authors describe this as delayed electrification linked to plume expansion and charge build-up. They also report that the duration of volcanic lightning varied from trivial to slightly longer than one day, typically within 12 hours.The study explains the delay in terms of the eruption's early stage. According to the authors, the initial phase is dominated by a rapid magmatic pyroclastic eruption, when charge separation efficiency is low even though the collision frequency between particles is very high. As the plume continues to rise, they write, volcanic gases are fully released and ionised. These gases combine with collisional charging of particles to build an electric field sufficient for dielectric breakdown.Why did wider ash plumes sustain volcanic lightning for longerThe duration of lightning activity was generally longer for eruptions with a large area of lightning activity, such as Cordón Caulle and Ulawun, and shorter for those with a small area, such as Raikoke. The authors report that the spatial extent of lightning also varied broadly, with half of the 16 eruptions (8) comparable to typical mesoscale convective systems. They conclude that ash dispersal controls "the persistence of electrification". In their explanation, the broader the spread of the plume, the wider the distribution of charged particles and the longer particle collisions and charge separation continue.The area of lightning activity was calculated by combining a convex hull method with DBSCAN clustering. The paper sets eps at 0.1 and min_samples at 10 for eruptions of VEI 5 or above, and 0.05 and 5 for those below VEI 5. To test these settings, the authors varied both parameters within 20 per cent of their baseline values. They report that the calculated area of the core lightning regions varied within 15 per cent and that the relative order of magnitude among eruptions stayed stable.Why did the Hunga Tonga eruption produce two peaks in lightning activityAccording to the authors, the Taal eruption in the Philippines began at about 06:40 UTC on 12 January 2020, and its plume reached roughly 17 km above sea level within about two hours. Lightning gradually intensified and then slowly weakened, lasting approximately 13 hours against an overall eruption duration of about 14 hours. Most detected lightning lay to the northeast of the volcano, with the main zone passing almost over Manila. The Hunga Tonga eruption of 15 January 2022 began at about 04:00 UTC, and the paper reports that its lightning reached a maximum within one hour. A second peak followed about four hours after the first, and the two outbreaks showed a nearly circular spatial distribution.The authors also linked the lightning to rainfall using Global Precipitation Measurement data. In both cases, they found a positive correlation between precipitation and lightning during the intensifying phase and a negative correlation after the lightning peak, which they attribute to precipitation-driven scavenging of charged particles. They report that the lightning enhancement rate rose with the Volcanic Explosivity Index. The method is most effective for explosive eruptions that produce substantial ash plumes, typically VEI 4 or above. Lightning signals may be weak or absent for phreatic or low-intensity eruptions, and the authors say real-time lightning data should be combined with observations such as satellite imagery and meteorological radar.

articles.title: Fossil kept in drawer for a century sheds light on enigmatic meat-eating dinosaurs
articles.summary: The partial skull of a tiger-sized predator that prowled what is now the Isle of Wight off England’s southern coast about 120 million years ago is giving scientists a better understanding of an enigmatic group of meat-eating dinosaurs known for running down prey and ripping them apart with massive hand claws.
articles.body: The partial skull of a tiger-sized predator that prowled what is now the Isle of Wight off England’s southern coast about 120 million years ago is giving scientists a better understanding of an enigmatic group of meat-eating dinosaurs known for running down prey and ripping them apart with massive hand claws. Researchers said the fossil belongs to a species they have named Invictibellatrix amberina, an early member of the lineage of Cretaceous Period carnivorous dinosaurs called megaraptorans. Invictibellatrix adds to the knowledge of skull anatomy among early megaraptorans and, being the first one known from Europe, helps show how the group spread globally. Invictibellatrix is one of the smallest megaraptorans. Based on fossils of closely related megaraptorans, the researchers estimated that Invictibellatrix was about 16 feet long, with the weight of a large tiger. Its body may have been covered in filament-like feathers, they said. Megaraptorans were part of the group called theropods that spans all the meat-eating dinosaurs. “Megaraptorans are very unique among theropods because they have relatively small and slender heads but had long and strong arms with massive hand claws as well as very lightly built skeletons,” said Cassius Morrison, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Leeds in England and lead author of the study published in the journal Royal Society Open Science. “These characteristics imply that megaraptorans were agile hunters capable of chasing down prey and using their large arms and claws to catch them and disembowel them using their hand claws,” Morrison said. The largest-known megaraptoran, named Maip, was about 33 feet long, inhabiting Patagonia during the twilight of the dinosaur age, about 50 million years after Invictibellatrix lived. Littler megaraptorans like Invictibellatrix may have hunted smaller prey like mammals, smaller reptiles and baby dinosaurs. Larger megaraptorans may have targeted bigger plant-eating dinosaurs like duckbilled hadrosaurs and long-necked sauropods, though probably not the biggest ones. Megaraptorans hunted in the opposite way from massive predators like Tyrannosaurus rex. Tyrannosaurus employed its large and stoutly built head, enormous teeth and incredible bite strength to kill prey, but had puny arms of little use in hunting. Invictibellatrix was not the Isle of Wight’s top predator, with larger theropods around, alongside various herbivorous dinosaurs, and may have filled a role similar to a hyena today. There is a debate among dinosaur paleontologists as to where megaraptorans fit on the theropod family tree. Despite differences in how they were built and hunted, one hypothesis is that megaraptorans were closely related to tyrannosaurs, the group that included Tyrannosaurus and others that dominated the landscapes in North America and Asia later in the Cretaceous. Invictibellatrix means “unconquered female warrior.” Morrison noted that after humble beginnings megaraptorans developed into apex predators in South America, Australia and Antarctica, becoming “the ruling queens,” while the tyrannosaurs became the “tyrant kings” in North America and Asia. Scientists are trying to unravel the evolutionary history of megaraptorans. A leading hypothesis has megaraptorans originating in Asia before migrating through Europe into Africa and then on into South America, thriving until the dinosaurs were doomed by an asteroid strike 66 million years ago. This hypothesis was lacking fossil evidence because no megaraptorans had been known from Europe until now. “These findings help to uncover the evolution of one of the most mysterious theropod groups,” University College London doctoral student and study co-author Charlie Scherer said. The Invictibellatrix fossil, a fragmented braincase, was discovered about a century ago and acquired by the Natural History Museum in London in 1924. “It was left in one of the collection’s drawers ever since, and no one noticed it until a couple of years ago,” Scherer said. While Tyrannosaurus may be more imposing than Invictibellatrix, the researchers noted that if a person were somehow transported back in time — like in the recent film “The End of Oak Street” — Invictibellatrix might present more of a danger. “A smaller theropod like Invictibellatrix would likely have been a much bigger threat to a human than something like T. rex because we would likely be too small for T. rex to see as a worthwhile meal because of how massive it was and the amount of energy it would be required to catch us,” Morrison said. “But we would be the perfect size for something smaller like Invictibellatrix, as we are about a third to a quarter of its weight, making us a good hearty meal and more than just a snack. Additionally, Invictibellatrix would have the agility and maneuverability to pursue and catch a human.”
